Precision@800 on a held-out day's scores, reported next to recall@800
F1 computed at the default 0.5 probability threshold
Log loss over all 400,000 scored items
mcq.rationale: Only the 800 highest-ranked items are ever acted on, so the metric must be evaluated at exactly that cut-off: precision@800 measures the share of the reviewers' effort that lands on genuine violations, and recall@800 measures how much of the day's violating content the budget captures. Metrics defined over the whole score distribution are dominated by regions of the ranking that no reviewer touches, so large changes there can leave the top 800 untouched and vice versa.
misconceptions: Picks a threshold-free ranking summary whose value is driven mostly by the tail no reviewer sees
CORRECT
Anchors evaluation to an arbitrary probability cut-off that bears no relation to a fixed 800-item capacity
Chooses a proper scoring rule that averages probability quality over the full distribution rather than top-of-ranking behaviour

mcq.stem: During error analysis of a production intent classifier you sample 200 misclassified validation utterances and hand-label the cause of each failure. 84 of the 200 turn out to be cases where the recorded ground-truth intent is itself wrong. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Increase model capacity, since 42% of the errors are patterns the current model cannot represent
Oversample the affected intents during training so the model sees more examples of these cases

Re-audit and correct the labels in the validation and test sets before comparing further model variants, since noisy ground truth caps measured performance and can invert the ranking of two candidates
Keep the labels as they are and report an adjusted accuracy by subtracting the mislabelled fraction from the measured error rate
mcq.rationale: When a large share of counted errors are annotation errors, the measured error rate is describing the evaluation set rather than the model: the ceiling on achievable accuracy is set by label noise, and because the noise is not uniform across models, two candidates whose true quality differs can swap places on the dirty split. Cleaning the eval labels restores the measurement before any modelling change is worth evaluating.
misconceptions: Reads label noise as an underfitting signal and reaches for capacity instead of fixing the measurement
Treats a label-quality problem as a class-imbalance problem, which trains the model to fit the wrong labels more confidently
CORRECT
Assumes label noise can be discounted arithmetically; the model is also wrong on some of those items, so the correction is neither uniform nor recoverable from the aggregate

mcq.stem: You apply temperature scaling to a multiclass image classifier: a single scalar `T` is fitted on a held-out calibration split by minimising NLL, and at inference the logits are divided by `T` before `softmax`. The fitted value is `T = 1.7`. What happens to the model's top-1 accuracy and its expected calibration error (ECE) on the test set?
options: Top-1 accuracy is unchanged, because dividing every logit by the same positive scalar preserves their ordering; ECE typically falls because the softened probabilities are less overconfident
Both fall, because shrinking the logits pushes the distribution toward uniform and costs the model decisions it previously got right
Top-1 accuracy improves, because the previously overconfident errors are reassigned to the correct class
Top-1 accuracy is unchanged and ECE is essentially unchanged, since ECE is determined by how the model ranks its predictions
mcq.rationale: Temperature scaling is a strictly monotone, order-preserving transform of the logits, so the `argmax` â€” and therefore every hard prediction and accuracy â€” is untouched. What it changes is the magnitude of the softmax output: `T > 1` indicates the network was overconfident, and flattening the distribution brings mean confidence per bin back toward observed accuracy, which is exactly what ECE measures.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes a positive monotone rescaling can change which class wins; it changes magnitudes, not ordering
Believes calibration re-orders class scores rather than re-mapping confidence onto the existing ordering
Confuses ECE with a rank-based metric such as AUC; ECE depends on the predicted probability values themselves, which is precisely what temperature changes

mcq.stem: A binary churn classifier is evaluated on a held-out set in which 4% of accounts actually churned. It reports 96% accuracy, and the confusion matrix shows it predicted the positive class zero times. What does the 96% figure tell you about the model's usefulness for retention outreach?
options: It confirms the model is well calibrated, since 96% accuracy matches the 96% negative base rate
It shows the model has learned the majority class well, so the remaining work is only to lift recall on the 4%
It indicates overfitting to the training set, which stronger regularisation would correct

Nothing useful â€” a constant 'no churn' predictor scores exactly the same, so under this class balance accuracy cannot separate a useful model from a trivial one; positive-class recall/precision or PR-AUC is needed
mcq.rationale: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class when the positive rate is 4%. A model that never predicts churn already achieves 96%, so that number carries no evidence that the model learned any churn signal, and it flags zero accounts for outreach. Metrics conditioned on the positive class â€” recall, precision, PR-AUC â€” are the ones that move when the model actually becomes useful.
misconceptions: Confuses a numerical coincidence between accuracy and the base rate with calibration, which is about predicted probabilities matching observed frequencies
Treats a majority-class score as evidence of learning; a constant predictor attains the same score, so no learning is demonstrated
Attributes a metric-choice and class-imbalance problem to variance; the symptom here appears on the evaluation set regardless of overfitting
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You need calibrated probabilities from a gradient-boosted trees classifier and have 800 held-out examples reserved for calibration. Using scikit-learn's `CalibratedClassifierCV`, you must choose between `method="sigmoid"` (Platt scaling) and `method="isotonic"`. Given that calibration-set size, which should you choose and why?
options: `isotonic`, because a non-parametric monotone fit dominates Platt scaling irrespective of calibration-set size

`sigmoid`, because Platt scaling estimates only two parameters and stays stable on small calibration sets, whereas isotonic regression's step function has effective complexity that grows with the data and overfits a few hundred points
Either one â€” `CalibratedClassifierCV` cross-validates internally, so calibration-set size does not affect the choice
`isotonic`, because Platt scaling assumes a sigmoid-shaped distortion and cannot correct a distortion running the other way
mcq.rationale: Platt scaling fits two parameters in `1 / (1 + exp(A*s + B))`, so its variance stays low on small samples at the cost of assuming a sigmoid-shaped distortion. Isotonic regression fits an arbitrary monotone step function whose number of steps grows with the data; with only a few hundred calibration points it places bin boundaries on noise and can end up with worse log loss than the uncalibrated scores. Isotonic becomes the better choice once the calibration set runs to thousands of examples.
misconceptions: Generalises isotonic regression's asymptotic flexibility to the small-sample regime, where its variance dominates its lower bias
CORRECT
Thinks internal cross-validation removes the calibrator's own variance; it only reuses the data to fit and average several calibrators, each still fitted on a small fold
Misstates Platt scaling's limitation as directional; the fitted slope and intercept let it sharpen or soften scores either way, and its real constraint is the sigmoid functional form

mcq.stem: You audit a loan-default classifier with Fairlearn. `demographic_parity_difference` comes out at `0.02` (inside your 0.05 tolerance) while `equalized_odds_difference` is `0.19`, and the observed default base rate differs substantially between the two groups being compared. What does this combination of results indicate about the model?
options: The audit is internally inconsistent â€” both metrics are derived from the same per-group confusion matrices, so a model passing demographic parity cannot show a large equalized-odds gap
The equalized-odds gap is an artefact of scoring on raw probabilities; recomputing both metrics from hard labels at a `0.5` threshold will bring them into agreement

The model equalises the rate at which each group is approved, but with unequal base rates that forces the groups' true-positive and false-positive rates apart â€” the two criteria cannot both hold except for a trivial or perfect classifier
The gap reflects estimator variance from the smaller group; weighting `equalized_odds_difference` by group size would bring it back inside tolerance
mcq.rationale: Demographic parity constrains the selection rate `P(Å¶=1 | A)`, while equalized odds constrains error rates conditioned on the true label. When base rates `P(Y=1 | A)` differ across groups, matching selection rates necessarily pushes TPR and FPR apart, so the two criteria are provably incompatible outside degenerate cases. The audit is not broken â€” it is surfacing a genuine trade-off that has to be resolved by choosing which criterion the deployment context requires.
misconceptions: Treats the fairness criteria as interchangeable and assumes satisfying one implies the other
Blames the discrepancy on thresholding rather than on the differing base rates that drive it
CORRECT
Confuses sampling noise in a small group with a structural incompatibility; equalized-odds difference is a max over groups, not a size-weighted average

mcq.stem: You explain an XGBoost churn model with `shap.TreeExplainer`. Two inputs, `tenure_days` and `n_invoices`, are correlated at `0.93`. In the global `mean(|SHAP|)` bar chart they rank adjacent with roughly equal magnitude, and each is about half the magnitude that the same feature receives in a model fitted on only one of them. A product manager reads this as 'each feature causes about half of the churn risk'. What is the correct technical objection to that reading?
options: SHAP attributes this particular fitted model's output across its inputs, so redundant correlated features split the credit according to how the trees happened to use them; the split is a property of the model, not a standalone predictive contribution or a causal effect in the world
`mean(|SHAP|)` values are not comparable between features unless the features are standardised to zero mean and unit variance before fitting, otherwise the larger-scale feature dominates the ranking
SHAP values are inherently local, so averaging their magnitudes across the dataset is not a defensible global summary; permutation importance is the only valid global ranking
Switching `TreeExplainer` to the interventional (background-dataset) estimator breaks the dependence between the two features and recovers each one's true independent contribution
mcq.rationale: Shapley attributions distribute the fitted model's output among its inputs. When two features carry near-identical information, the trees split their reliance between them, and a refit on the same data can reallocate that split without changing predictions. Attribution therefore describes model reliance, and cannot be read as a causal claim about churn.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Thinks SHAP values inherit input feature scale, when they are expressed in units of the model output
Over-applies the local nature of SHAP; mean absolute SHAP is a standard and valid global summary
Believes the interventional masking convention recovers causal or independent effects rather than simply changing how credit is shared among correlated features

mcq.stem: A voice-intent classifier reports `94%` accuracy on your held-out test set. Before shipping, you need evidence that it does not fail disproportionately for particular user populations or recording conditions. Which evaluation produces that evidence?
options: Enlarge the test set until the confidence interval on overall accuracy is narrower than `0.5%`
Refit with class weights so the majority intent no longer dominates the headline number
Replace accuracy with macro-averaged F1 so every class contributes equally to the score
Disaggregate the metric into slices â€” by accent, device type, and background-noise level â€” and report each slice's score with a confidence interval
mcq.rationale: An aggregate score is a weighted average over the test distribution, so a severe failure on a small population is invisible in it no matter how precisely it is estimated. Only computing the metric separately on the slices you care about, with intervals that expose thin slices, gives the required evidence.
misconceptions: Confuses precision of the aggregate estimate with coverage of subgroups; a tighter interval on a masked average still hides slice failures
Proposes a training-time mitigation instead of an evaluation, and targets label imbalance rather than population subgroups
Averages over output classes rather than over user populations, which is a different axis entirely
CORRECT

mcq.stem: The partial dependence plot for `income` on your gradient-boosted risk model is essentially flat, yet the feature ranks high in permutation importance. You plot individual conditional expectation (ICE) curves for the same feature and see steep upward curves for roughly half the rows and steep downward curves for the rest. What does this pattern tell you?
options: The model has underfit `income`; the individual curves are noise from insufficient regularisation, and the flat PDP is the reliable summary
A PDP is the pointwise average of the ICE curves, so opposing per-row effects cancel â€” `income` has a strong but direction-reversing effect driven by an interaction with another feature
The ICE curves are evaluated at feature combinations outside the training data's support, so their slopes are extrapolation artefacts and the PDP should be trusted
`income` is strongly correlated with another feature, so its effect is shared between them; centring the ICE curves at the minimum value of `income` would make the PDP non-flat
mcq.rationale: Partial dependence at each grid point is the mean of the ICE values there, so subgroups with opposite-signed effects cancel and produce a flat curve. A bidirectional ICE fan is the classic signature of an interaction, and the next step is to condition or colour the ICE curves on the suspected moderating feature.
misconceptions: Reads a flat PDP as evidence the model barely uses the feature, contradicting the permutation-importance result in the stem
CORRECT
Invokes a real PDP/ICE caveat but one that would not produce a systematic split into two opposite-signed groups
Confuses correlation-driven credit sharing with an interaction, and assumes centring changes the average rather than only the vertical offset of each curve

mcq.stem: A PyTorch training loop calls `loss.backward()` and `optimizer.step()` on every mini-batch but never calls `optimizer.zero_grad()`. What effect does this have on the parameter updates?
options: Nothing measurable â€” `loss.backward()` overwrites `.grad` on each call, so `zero_grad()` only matters when swapping optimizers
After the first `step()` the `.grad` tensors are released and become `None`, so parameters stop updating altogether
`.grad` accumulates, so each update is driven by the running sum of every earlier batch's gradient; the effective step grows without bound and training diverges
Only the final layer is affected, because the graph buffers for the earlier layers are freed at the end of each `backward()`
mcq.rationale: `backward()` adds into the existing `.grad` of each leaf tensor rather than replacing it â€” that accumulation is what makes manual gradient accumulation across micro-batches possible. Without `zero_grad()` the accumulated sum keeps growing, so `step()` applies an ever-larger update in a stale averaged direction.
misconceptions: Believes `backward()` assigns to `.grad` instead of accumulating into it
Confuses `zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` freeing the buffers with the consequence of never calling it at all
CORRECT
Conflates freeing the intermediate autograd graph with the persistence of leaf `.grad` tensors

mcq.stem: An engineer tracks epoch loss with `epoch_loss += loss` inside the batch loop, where `loss` is the tensor returned by the criterion. GPU memory climbs steadily across the epoch and the run OOMs partway through, even though batch size and model are unchanged from a working version. What is the mechanism?
options: `epoch_loss` still references each batch's autograd graph, so the activations of every processed batch are kept alive instead of being freed after `backward()`
Summing tensors on the GPU forces a device-to-device copy per batch, and the allocator cannot reuse those blocks until the epoch ends
The optimizer's momentum buffers grow by one entry per batch because the running loss is registered as an extra parameter
Adding a scalar tensor to a Python float promotes `epoch_loss` to `float64`, doubling the memory of every activation downstream
mcq.rationale: A loss tensor carries `grad_fn`, so holding a reference to it keeps its whole graph â€” and the saved activations it points to â€” reachable. Normally those buffers are freed once `backward()` completes and the last reference drops; accumulating the tensor instead of `loss.item()` or `loss.detach()` pins one graph per batch.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Invents an allocator/copy explanation for what is a reference-retention problem
Confuses optimizer state, which is sized by parameter count, with per-batch graph retention
Misattributes activation memory growth to scalar dtype promotion, which affects only the accumulator itself

mcq.stem: A teammate builds a classifier as three stacked `nn.Linear` layers with no activation function between them, followed by a softmax output, and reports it performs no better than plain logistic regression no matter how wide the hidden layers are. What explains this?
options: Without activations the layers saturate at initialisation, so widening helps only after batch normalisation is inserted
The hidden layers are too narrow relative to the input; sufficient width alone would give the model nonlinear decision boundaries
Backpropagation cannot pass through a layer that has no activation, so only the final linear layer actually receives gradient
Composing affine maps yields another affine map, so the three layers collapse to one equivalent `nn.Linear` â€” depth and width add no expressive power
mcq.rationale: `W3(W2(W1x + b1) + b2) + b3` can be rewritten as `Wx + b` with `W = W3W2W1`. The nonlinearity between layers is what makes stacking increase the function class; without it the network's hypothesis space is exactly that of a single linear layer.
misconceptions: Attributes a representational limit to an optimisation pathology that normalisation would fix
Confuses width (capacity within a function class) with the nonlinearity that changes the function class
Believes activation functions are required for gradient flow rather than for expressiveness
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You are budgeting memory for a CNN head. After flattening a `256 x 7 x 7` feature map you attach `nn.Linear(12544, 1024)` with its default `bias=True`. How many trainable parameters does that single layer contribute, as `sum(p.numel() for p in layer.parameters())` would report?
mcq.rationale: A fully connected layer holds a `1024 x 12544` weight matrix (12,845,056 entries) plus a bias vector of 1024, giving 12,846,080. The bias term is small here but the weight matrix alone explains why the first dense layer after a flatten usually dominates a CNN's parameter count.
misconceptions: Counts the weight matrix but omits the bias vector that `bias=True` allocates
CORRECT
Adds the fan-in and fan-out instead of multiplying, treating the layer as one parameter per unit rather than per connection
Counts the gradient buffer alongside the weights; `parameters()` reports each trainable tensor once

mcq.stem: Fine-tuning a deep transformer OOMs at the batch size you need, and profiling shows stored activations â€” not parameters or optimizer state â€” dominate memory. You wrap the encoder blocks in `torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint`. What does this change at the mechanism level?
options: Gradients are computed in half precision inside the wrapped blocks and cast back afterwards, halving the memory those activations occupy
The wrapped blocks' activations are offloaded to CPU RAM during the forward pass and streamed back over PCIe when backward reaches them

Intermediate activations inside a wrapped block are discarded after the forward pass and recomputed by re-running that block's forward during backward, trading roughly one extra forward pass for the memory
Parameters and their gradients are sharded across data-parallel ranks so each device holds only its slice of the encoder
mcq.rationale: Checkpointing runs the wrapped segment under `no_grad`, keeping only its inputs, then re-executes the forward inside `backward()` to regenerate the activations needed for the local gradient computation. Activation memory drops from every intermediate tensor to just the segment boundaries, at a compute cost of roughly one additional forward pass.
misconceptions: Confuses activation checkpointing with mixed-precision training, a separate and composable technique
Confuses checkpointing with activation/CPU offloading, which moves tensors rather than discarding and recomputing them
CORRECT
Confuses checkpointing with ZeRO-style sharding, which targets parameter and optimizer state rather than activations

mcq.stem: A PyTorch image classifier ends with `nn.Linear(512, 10)` followed by `nn.Softmax(dim=1)`, and the training loop computes `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(model(x), y)` with `y` as integer class indices. Training runs without error but converges very slowly and plateaus at poor accuracy. What is the mechanism behind this?
options: `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` requires one-hot targets, so passing integer class indices silently mis-scales the per-sample loss
`nn.Softmax(dim=1)` normalises across the batch dimension rather than the class dimension, mixing examples together

`nn.CrossEntropyLoss` already applies `log_softmax` internally, so the probabilities are softmaxed a second time; the effective score range collapses toward uniform and the gradients reaching the network are heavily damped
Softmax outputs are bounded in (0, 1), so the loss can never drop below `log(10)` no matter how well the network separates the classes
mcq.rationale: `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` is defined on raw logits: it fuses `log_softmax` with `nll_loss` for numerical stability. Feeding it softmax outputs means values already squeezed into (0, 1) are treated as logits and normalised again, so the largest achievable gap between class scores is tiny and the gradient signal is proportionally weak. The fix is to return raw logits from the model and delete the `nn.Softmax` layer.
misconceptions: Believes `CrossEntropyLoss` needs one-hot targets, when it accepts class indices directly by design
Misreads the `dim` argument â€” for an `(N, C)` tensor `dim=1` is the class axis, so the softmax is over the right axis
CORRECT
Invents a hard floor on the loss from bounded outputs instead of tracing the effect on the gradient

mcq.stem: A fraud detector is a binary classifier trained on a 1:1000 positive:negative split with `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=torch.tensor([50.0]))`. Recall improves markedly, but the downstream risk engine â€” which reads the `sigmoid` output as a probability of fraud â€” now reports expected losses far above realised losses, and a reliability diagram shows predicted probabilities above observed frequencies in every bin. What explains this, and what is the principled fix?
options: `pos_weight` multiplies the positive term of the loss, which moves the loss minimum itself: the network converges to the posterior under an artificially enriched positive prior, shifting every logit up by `log(pos_weight)`. Subtract that constant from the logit, or fit a calibrator on a held-out set carrying the true class balance.

Class weighting only rescales gradient magnitudes and leaves the minimiser unchanged, so the miscalibration must come from overfitting; adding weight decay and early stopping will realign the probabilities.

A `sigmoid` output is an unnormalised score, not a probability, so no probabilistic reading of it is ever valid; the risk engine should consume ranks only and the expected-loss calculation should be dropped.
Under weighting, `0.5` is no longer the Bayes-optimal operating point; raising the decision threshold to `pos_weight / (1 + pos_weight)` will flatten the reliability diagram.
mcq.rationale: Unweighted binary cross-entropy is a proper scoring rule: its minimiser at each input is the true conditional probability. Multiplying the positive term by `w` changes the stationary point to `q / (1 - q) = w * p / (1 - p)`, i.e. an additive `log(w)` offset in logit space, so outputs are systematically too high. Removing that offset â€” or post-hoc calibration on data with the deployment prior â€” restores probabilities; changing the threshold only moves the operating point and leaves the estimates biased.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Treats class weighting as a pure gradient-scale change, missing that it relocates the optimum of the loss
Denies that a cross-entropy-trained sigmoid estimates a posterior probability, discarding the proper-scoring-rule property that makes calibration meaningful
Confuses choosing a decision threshold with recalibrating the probability estimates a reliability diagram measures

mcq.stem: You are building a photo tagger where one image may legitimately carry several of 20 tags at once (`beach`, `sunset`, `people`, ...). The current head applies `softmax` over the 20 outputs and trains with categorical cross-entropy against a multi-hot target. Which output-and-loss combination fits this task?
options: Keep `softmax` but normalise each multi-hot target to sum to 1, so the target is a valid distribution
Keep `softmax` and raise the temperature, so several tags can score highly at the same time
Keep `softmax` but switch the loss to mean squared error, so the tags stop competing
Apply an independent `sigmoid` to each of the 20 logits and train with per-tag binary cross-entropy (`BCEWithLogitsLoss`)
mcq.rationale: `softmax` couples the outputs through a sum-to-one constraint, so raising confidence in one tag necessarily lowers the others â€” wrong when labels are not mutually exclusive. Modelling each tag as its own Bernoulli variable with a `sigmoid` and a per-tag binary cross-entropy lets any number of tags be confidently on, and thresholding is then done per tag.
misconceptions: Patches the target format while leaving the mutually-exclusive coupling imposed by `softmax` untouched
Thinks temperature relaxes the sum-to-one constraint; it only flattens the distribution, and the tags still compete for a fixed budget
Assumes changing the loss decouples the outputs, when the normalisation is imposed by the `softmax` layer itself
CORRECT

mcq.stem: A ViT fine-tuning script uses `torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.05)`, copying the coefficient straight from a paper whose authors trained with `AdamW`. Regularisation is visibly weaker than reported and the model overfits. What is the substantive difference between `weight_decay` in `Adam` and in `AdamW`?
options: None that matters at the algorithm level â€” `AdamW` is a fused, faster implementation of the same update, so identical `weight_decay` values give identical results
`AdamW` automatically exempts biases and normalisation parameters from decay, whereas `Adam` decays every tensor in the parameter group

`Adam` folds the decay into the gradient, so it is then divided by the adaptive second-moment denominator and parameters with large gradient magnitudes shrink least; `AdamW` subtracts `lr * weight_decay * Î¸` outside the adaptive rescaling, so every parameter shrinks by the same relative amount
`AdamW` multiplies its decay term by the current learning rate while `Adam` does not, so the coefficient must be rescaled by `1/lr` when switching optimisers
mcq.rationale: `Adam`'s `weight_decay` is classic L2: the term `wd * Î¸` is added to the gradient and therefore passes through the `/(sqrt(v_hat) + eps)` normalisation, so parameters with a large second-moment estimate receive far less effective decay â€” the coefficient no longer means a fixed shrinkage rate. `AdamW` decouples it, applying `Î¸ â† Î¸ - lr * wd * Î¸` as a separate step, which is why published `AdamW` coefficients do not transfer to `Adam`.
misconceptions: Treats decoupled weight decay as an implementation detail rather than a change to the update rule itself
Confuses the parameter-group convention hand-written in reference training scripts with behaviour built into `AdamW`
CORRECT
Half-remembers that decoupled decay is scaled by the learning rate and wrongly concludes the coefficient needs rescaling by `1/lr`

mcq.stem: A training run accumulates gradients over 8 micro-batches per optimiser update and is planned for 10,000 optimiser updates. You build a linear-warmup-then-cosine scheduler with `num_warmup_steps=500` and `num_training_steps=10000`, but place `scheduler.step()` inside the micro-batch loop instead of alongside `optimizer.step()`. What is the consequence for the learning-rate trajectory?
options: Nothing meaningful â€” `scheduler.step()` only writes `param_groups[i]['lr']`, which is read at `optimizer.step()`, so the extra calls are absorbed
The peak learning rate ends up 8Ã— higher than configured, because the warmup ramp is applied once per micro-batch and overshoots its target value
PyTorch raises a `RuntimeError` on the second `scheduler.step()` within one optimiser update, since schedulers assert exactly one step per update
The schedule is traversed 8Ã— too fast: warmup completes after roughly 62 optimiser updates instead of 500, and the cosine decay is exhausted about one-eighth of the way through training
mcq.rationale: A scheduler advances its own `last_epoch` counter on every `step()` call and is otherwise blind to whether the optimiser actually updated weights. Calling it 8Ã— per optimiser update consumes 8,000 of the 10,000 scheduled positions in the first 1,000 real updates, so the model spends almost all of training outside the intended schedule â€” the fix is to gate `scheduler.step()` on the same condition as `optimizer.step()`.
misconceptions: Thinks the scheduler is inert unless `optimizer.step()` runs; the internal step counter advances regardless of whether weights changed
Assumes the warmup ramp compounds past its endpoint; the warmup factor is bounded at 1.0 and cannot exceed the configured peak
Mistakes the advisory ordering warning PyTorch emits for a hard runtime assertion on step counts
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You attach `torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode="min", factor=0.5, patience=3)` to a PyTorch training loop so the learning rate is halved when validation loss stops improving. Where in the loop must it be stepped, and with what argument?
options: `scheduler.step()` immediately after every `optimizer.step()`, exactly like the other PyTorch schedulers
`scheduler.step(val_loss)` once per epoch, after the validation pass has produced the metric
`scheduler.step(train_loss)` after every mini-batch, so a plateau is detected as early as possible
No extra call is needed â€” `ReduceLROnPlateau` hooks into the optimiser and observes the loss automatically
mcq.rationale: `ReduceLROnPlateau` is metric-driven, not iteration-driven: `step()` takes the monitored quantity as a required argument and each call counts as one observation against `patience`. Feeding it the epoch's validation loss makes `patience=3` mean three epochs without improvement, which is what the hyperparameter is intended to express.
misconceptions: Treats it like an epoch- or iteration-driven scheduler; `step()` requires the metric positionally and calling it bare raises `TypeError`
CORRECT
Feeds a noisy per-batch training loss, so `patience` counts mini-batches and the learning rate collapses long before a real plateau
Assumes the scheduler can observe the loss on its own; PyTorch schedulers only see what `step()` is given and only mutate `param_groups`

mcq.stem: You instrument the forward pass of a 30-layer fully connected ReLU network whose weights were set with `nn.init.xavier_normal_`. On a single batch, the standard deviation of the activations drops by roughly a factor of `sqrt(2)` per layer, so the deepest layers output near-zero values and their gradients vanish. Which change to the initialisation fixes the cause?
options: Re-initialise with `nn.init.xavier_uniform_` instead, since the uniform variant draws larger magnitudes and preserves signal through depth
Re-initialise each weight matrix with the LeCun scaling `Var(w) = 1 / fan_in`, which is the variance-preserving choice for deep stacks
Re-initialise with `nn.init.kaiming_normal_(w, mode='fan_in', nonlinearity='relu')`, whose `2 / fan_in` variance compensates for ReLU zeroing half its inputs
Keep Xavier but initialise every bias to a small positive constant such as `0.01`, so fewer ReLU units sit in their inactive region
mcq.rationale: Xavier targets `Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out)`, which for square layers is `1 / fan_in` â€” variance-preserving only for an activation that is roughly linear about zero. ReLU discards the negative half, halving the variance at every layer, so activations decay geometrically. He (Kaiming) init doubles the weight variance to `2 / fan_in` precisely to cancel that factor of one half.
misconceptions: Believes the sampling distribution's shape changes the variance; the uniform and normal Xavier variants target the same variance
Applies LeCun scaling, which is derived for linear/tanh-like activations and leaves the same factor-of-two shrinkage per ReLU layer
CORRECT
Confuses a dead-ReLU mitigation with variance scaling; a constant bias shifts activations but does not restore the per-layer variance

mcq.stem: You fine-tune a pretrained ResNet-50 on a new imaging domain. To freeze the backbone you loop over `backbone.parameters()` and set `requires_grad = False`, then train only a fresh classification head. Training loss falls as expected, but when you later run the backbone under `model.eval()` on the original validation images, its feature outputs no longer match the pretrained checkpoint's â€” even though a state-dict diff shows no backbone weight has changed. What accounts for the drift?
options: The `BatchNorm2d` layers were left in training mode, so each forward pass kept updating their `running_mean` and `running_var` buffers, which `requires_grad` does not govern
BatchNorm's `weight` and `bias` are registered as buffers rather than parameters, so iterating `backbone.parameters()` never froze the affine transform
The optimiser continues to apply weight decay and momentum to the frozen tensors each step, shrinking them even with no gradient signal
Dropout inside the backbone remained active, so the backbone's outputs are stochastic rather than drifted
mcq.rationale: `requires_grad` only controls gradient-based updates to parameters. A BatchNorm layer in training mode normalises with the current batch statistics and separately updates its running-statistics buffers by exponential moving average as a side effect of the forward pass. Those buffers are what eval mode uses, so they migrate toward the new domain. Freezing a backbone that contains BN requires putting the BN modules into `eval()` mode as well.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses BN's learnable affine parameters, which `parameters()` does cover, with its non-learnable running-statistics buffers, which it does not
Does not know PyTorch optimisers skip parameters whose `.grad` is `None`, so frozen tensors receive no decay or momentum update
Attributes a deterministic shift in eval-mode features to stochastic regularisation, and assumes a residual CNN backbone contains dropout

mcq.stem: A teammate initialises every weight matrix of a fully connected ReLU classifier to zeros, reasoning that gradient descent will pull them apart within an epoch. Training runs without error but accuracy stays at chance no matter how long it runs. What is the underlying problem?
options: Zeroed weights place every ReLU exactly on its non-differentiable kink, so autograd propagates `NaN` and no update is applied
Zero initialisation is only harmful for biases; zeroing weight matrices is standard practice, so the fault lies with the learning rate or optimiser
The network simply needs far more epochs, because gradient descent must first grow the weights away from the origin before learning begins
Every unit within a layer computes the same output and therefore receives the same gradient, so the units stay identical forever and the layer can only ever represent one feature
mcq.rationale: Random initialisation exists to break symmetry. With identical incoming weights, all units in a layer are indistinguishable in both the forward and backward pass, so their updates are identical at every step and they remain a single duplicated feature. The problem is structural, not a matter of scale or patience.
misconceptions: Invents a differentiability failure; the sub-gradient at zero is well defined and no `NaN` arises
Inverts the rule: zero biases are safe, zero weights are not, since it is the weights that must break symmetry
Believes SGD eventually breaks the tie, missing that identical units receive identical gradients at every step
CORRECT

mcq.stem: In code review of a block written as `nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1, bias=True)` followed immediately by `nn.BatchNorm2d(128)`, a reviewer asks you to pass `bias=False` to the convolution. What is the technical justification?
options: Without it, the bias offset inflates BatchNorm's `running_var`, so eval-time normalisation is scaled incorrectly
BatchNorm subtracts the per-channel mean, so the constant the conv bias adds cancels exactly; its gradient is zero and its role is already played by BatchNorm's learnable `beta`
The conv bias prevents BatchNorm from being folded into the convolution weights at inference, blocking that deployment optimisation
The two offsets compete for the same degree of freedom, which makes the block ill-conditioned and slows convergence
mcq.rationale: BatchNorm's output is invariant to any per-channel constant added to its input, because that constant appears in both the activation and the batch mean and cancels in the subtraction. The conv bias therefore has an exactly zero gradient and no effect on the function computed â€” it is inert parameter and optimiser state, and the shift the block needs is supplied by `beta`.
misconceptions: Thinks a constant offset changes the variance; adding a constant shifts the mean only and leaves the variance untouched
CORRECT
Believes a conv bias blocks BN folding, whereas folding absorbs conv bias, `gamma`, `beta` and the running statistics into a single weight-and-bias pair
Assumes the redundancy actively harms optimisation, when the cancelled bias receives no gradient at all and cannot fight `beta`

mcq.stem: A very deep pre-activation ResNet diverges within the first few hundred steps at the large learning rate your schedule calls for. A standard remedy is to initialise the `weight` (the `gamma` scale) of the last `BatchNorm` inside every residual block to `0` instead of `1`, leaving all other initialisation unchanged. What does this achieve?
options: Setting `gamma` to zero puts those BatchNorm layers into a pass-through mode, so activations are left un-normalised through the unstable early steps
Zero is a fixed point for `gamma` â€” its gradient vanishes there â€” so the residual branch stays switched off and the effective depth is permanently reduced
Every residual block starts out as an exact identity map, so the signal variance no longer compounds with depth at step 0 and the branches are phased in as `gamma` grows
It centres the residual branch's output, removing the mean shift that would otherwise accumulate across hundreds of stacked blocks
mcq.rationale: With the block's final `gamma` at zero the branch contributes nothing, so the block output equals its input and the whole network reduces to the identity path at initialisation. Forward variance and backward gradient norms then stay flat with depth instead of compounding, which is what allows a large learning rate to survive the first steps. `gamma` is not stuck: its gradient is the loss gradient dotted with the non-zero normalised activation, so the branches switch on progressively as training proceeds.
misconceptions: Confuses zeroing the affine scale with disabling normalisation; the layer still subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation
Mistakes zero `gamma` for a symmetry-style fixed point, missing that its gradient depends on the non-zero normalised activation it multiplies
CORRECT
Confuses the scale `gamma` with the shift `beta`, and overlooks that BatchNorm has already centred the branch output

mcq.stem: You fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 backbone for detection at high input resolution, so GPU memory limits you to `batch_size=2` per device. Training loss falls smoothly, but validation mAP scored with `model.eval()` is far worse than the mAP obtained on the *same* validation images with the model left in `model.train()` mode, and it swings widely between neighbouring checkpoints. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too large for a batch of 2, so the weights oscillate; rescaling it by the linear scaling rule will close the gap
Weight decay is being applied to the BatchNorm affine parameters, driving `gamma` toward zero and killing the signal

Each BatchNorm layer normalises over only 2 samples, so its batch statistics are extremely noisy and the running mean/var buffers that `eval()` substitutes are a poor estimate of the true activation statistics
`model.eval()` additionally disables gradient tracking, so the forward pass follows a different numerical path than in training
mcq.rationale: BatchNorm behaves differently in the two modes: in training it normalises with the statistics of the current mini-batch, in eval it uses the accumulated running estimates. With only 2 samples per batch the per-step statistics are high-variance, so the EMA buffers converge poorly and drift between checkpoints â€” which is exactly why small-batch fine-tuning either freezes BN at the pretrained statistics (`bn.eval()` plus frozen affine params) or replaces it with GroupNorm, whose normalisation is per-sample and batch-size independent.
misconceptions: Reads a train-vs-eval mode discrepancy as an optimisation-stability problem, though a bad learning rate would degrade both modes equally
Recalls the real practice of excluding norm parameters from weight decay but misapplies it: shrinking `gamma` hurts training and eval identically, it does not open a gap between them
CORRECT
Confuses `model.eval()` with `torch.no_grad()`; `eval()` only switches BatchNorm and Dropout behaviour and does not change gradient tracking

mcq.stem: A U-Net segmentation decoder upsamples with `nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_ch, out_ch, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1)`. The predicted masks contain a regular high-frequency grid of brighter and darker pixels that survives long training and appears across all classes. What is the mechanism, and which change eliminates it?
options: Because `kernel_size` is not divisible by `stride`, output positions receive unequal numbers of kernel contributions, baking a fixed periodic pattern into every feature map; use `kernel_size=4` with `stride=2`, or replace the layer with nearest/bilinear upsampling followed by a `3x3` convolution
The stride-2 convolutions in the encoder alias high-frequency content, and the decoder amplifies it; insert a blur (anti-aliased downsampling) before each encoder stride
The final `sigmoid` is saturating on an imbalanced foreground/background split, so per-pixel logits quantise; switch the loss from BCE to Dice
The skip connections concatenate encoder and decoder tensors at mismatched spatial resolutions; interpolate the encoder features to the decoder size before concatenating
mcq.rationale: A transposed convolution scatters each input activation over a `kernel_size` window with step `stride`. When `stride` does not divide `kernel_size` evenly, the scattered windows overlap non-uniformly, so some output pixels accumulate more kernel taps than their neighbours â€” a deterministic checkerboard that gradient descent cannot fully absorb because it is a property of the layer's geometry, not of its weights. Making `kernel_size` a multiple of `stride` equalises the overlap, and resize-then-convolve avoids the scatter operation entirely.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Attributes a decoder upsampling artefact to encoder aliasing; anti-aliased downsampling addresses shift-instability and texture aliasing, not a fixed output-side grid
Treats a deterministic spatial artefact as a loss/calibration problem, which would change mask sharpness or boundaries but not impose a periodic pixel lattice
Confuses uneven kernel overlap with a shape-mismatch bug, which in PyTorch would raise a size error at `torch.cat` rather than produce a regular grid

mcq.stem: You classify variable-length product reviews by feeding a right-padded batch into `nn.LSTM` and passing the final hidden state `h_n` to a linear head. Accuracy on short reviews is far worse than on long ones. What is the correct fix?
options: Set `bidirectional=True` and concatenate both directions' `h_n`, so the reverse pass compensates for the trailing positions
Give `nn.Embedding` a `padding_idx=0`, so the zeroed pad embeddings leave the recurrent state untouched
Wrap the batch in `nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence` with the true lengths, so the LSTM stops at each sequence's last real token and `h_n` is that token's state
Mask the padded positions out of the loss with `ignore_index` in `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`
mcq.rationale: With right padding the LSTM keeps stepping over pad tokens, so `h_n` is the state after the padding rather than after the last real token â€” and the more padding a sequence carries, the more its representation drifts, which is why short reviews suffer most. Packing tells cuDNN each sequence's true length so `h_n` is taken at that boundary.
misconceptions: Treats a padding-contamination bug as a modelling-capacity gap; the reverse direction starts on padding and is corrupted the same way
Assumes a zero-valued input makes a recurrent step a no-op, forgetting the gates still update the state from `h_{t-1}` and the bias terms
CORRECT
Applies output-side masking to a problem in the recurrent state; with one label per sequence there are no padded targets to mask

mcq.stem: An LSTM sequence tagger trained on 400-step inputs learns local patterns but never captures dependencies more than roughly 20 steps back, and logged per-timestep gradient norms decay sharply toward the start of each sequence. Which change most directly targets the mechanism producing this?
options: Initialise the forget-gate bias to a positive constant such as `1.0`, so the cell state defaults to retention and the additive carry path stays open early in training
Lower the `clip_grad_norm_` threshold so the updates stay better conditioned across timesteps
Increase `hidden_size` so the cell has enough capacity to hold long-range context
Replace the cell's `tanh` candidate nonlinearity with `ReLU`, whose derivative does not saturate below 1
mcq.rationale: The cell state's gradient is carried backwards multiplied by the forget gate at each step. With zero-initialised biases the gate sits near `sigmoid(0) = 0.5`, so the signal is roughly halved per timestep and is effectively gone after a couple of dozen steps. A positive forget bias pushes the gate near 1 at initialisation, keeping the near-identity carry path intact until the gates learn when to close.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Prescribes the remedy for exploding gradients when the logged symptom is vanishing ones; clipping only ever scales large norms down
Reads a gradient-propagation failure as a parameter-count shortfall, when the signal never reaches the early steps to be stored
Transplants a feedforward vanishing-gradient fix into a recurrent cell, where an unbounded candidate destabilises the state and leaves the multiplicative forget-gate path untouched

mcq.stem: Your speech model uses `nn.LSTM(..., bidirectional=True)` and scores well offline. Product now requires live captions that appear while the speaker is still talking. Why can this architecture not be deployed as-is?
options: It doubles the parameter count, so the per-frame compute exceeds the real-time budget
It requires `batch_first=True`, which cannot be used with a single streaming sequence
It works once you reset the initial hidden state to zeros at the start of each incoming audio chunk
The backward layer reads the sequence from the last frame to the first, so no output for any frame exists until the utterance has finished
mcq.rationale: A bidirectional layer's output at time `t` concatenates a forward state that depends on frames `1..t` with a backward state that depends on frames `T..t`. The backward half is not computable until the final frame arrives, which makes the model non-causal and therefore unusable for incremental decoding regardless of how fast it runs.
misconceptions: Frames a hard causality constraint as a throughput problem, which faster hardware would then solve
Confuses a tensor-layout flag with the direction in which the recurrence is unrolled
Believes re-initialising state per chunk makes the backward direction causal, when it still needs that chunk's future frames
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Shrinking an on-device keyword-spotting model, you swap `nn.LSTM(input_size=64, hidden_size=256)` for `nn.GRU(input_size=64, hidden_size=256)`. How does the recurrent layer's weight count change, and why?
options: It is unchanged, because both allocate `weight_ih_l0` and `weight_hh_l0` with `4 * hidden_size` rows
It falls to roughly three quarters, because the GRU computes three weight blocks (reset, update, candidate) where the LSTM computes four (input, forget, output, candidate)
It halves, because the GRU's two gates replace the LSTM's four gates
It grows slightly, because the GRU needs an extra projection to recover the cell state that the LSTM stores separately
mcq.rationale: Both cells pack their per-step transforms into two matrices, but the LSTM stacks four blocks and the GRU three, so `weight_ih_l0` is `[4H, input]` versus `[3H, input]` and `weight_hh_l0` is `[4H, H]` versus `[3H, H]`. The ratio is 3/4 at equal `hidden_size`; the absent cell state costs no parameters because it is only a state vector.
misconceptions: Assumes the LSTM's `4 *` weight packing is a property of all gated cells rather than of its four blocks
CORRECT
Counts gates alone, treating the LSTM's candidate transform as a gate and ignoring that the GRU also has a candidate block
Invents a learned projection for the cell state; the GRU simply carries a single hidden vector and has nothing to reconstruct

mcq.stem: Training a stateful character-level LM, you carry the LSTM hidden state across consecutive chunks of one long document and call `loss.backward()` once per chunk. From the second chunk onward you hit `RuntimeError: Trying to backward through the graph a second time`, and memory climbs steadily. You want to keep the cross-chunk context but bound backpropagation to a single chunk. What do you do?
options: Call `loss.backward(retain_graph=True)` so the earlier chunk's graph survives into the next iteration
Re-initialise `h` and `c` to zeros at the start of every chunk
Carry the state forward detached, e.g. `h = tuple(t.detach() for t in h)`, so the numeric state persists while the autograd graph is cut at the chunk boundary
Move `optimizer.zero_grad()` to before the forward pass rather than after `optimizer.step()`
mcq.rationale: The returned hidden state is a tensor node still attached to the previous chunk's graph, so the next `backward()` walks back into buffers already freed. Detaching keeps the same numeric values â€” the model still sees the earlier context â€” but makes the state a graph leaf, which is exactly the truncation that truncated BPTT is defined by.
misconceptions: Silences the error by never freeing the graph, so the backward path and activation memory grow with every chunk processed
Fixes the graph problem by discarding precisely the carried-over context that the stateful setup exists to provide
CORRECT
Confuses accumulated `.grad` buffers with a retained autograd graph; zeroing gradients at either point frees no activations

mcq.stem: A 32-head decoder-only model is served with `n_heads = 32` and `n_kv_heads = 32`, and profiling shows the KV cache dominates GPU memory at long context. You retrain it as a grouped-query attention (GQA) model with `n_kv_heads = 8`, leaving `n_heads = 32` and `head_dim` unchanged. What is the principal effect on serving?
options: Attention FLOPs fall roughly 4x, because the number of query-key dot products is divided by the group count
Total parameter count falls roughly 4x, because every attention projection shrinks with the group count
Per-token KV cache memory falls roughly 4x, because only 8 key/value head pairs are stored while all 32 query heads attend to them
Memory per sequence becomes linear rather than quadratic in sequence length
mcq.rationale: GQA reduces only the number of distinct K/V projections; each group of 4 query heads reads the same cached K/V pair. Every query head still computes a full score row, so score/attention FLOPs are unchanged â€” the win is 4x less cached K/V state per token, which is exactly what a memory-bound decode loop is limited by.
misconceptions: Assumes sharing K/V also removes query-side compute; all 32 query heads still attend, so attention FLOPs are essentially unchanged
Applies the K/V reduction to the query and output projections and the FFN, which dominate parameters and are untouched
CORRECT
Confuses shrinking the constant factor of the KV cache with changing an asymptotic; the cache was already linear in sequence length

mcq.stem: An 8k-context training run OOMs inside the attention block. Swapping the naive `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) @ V` implementation for a FlashAttention kernel makes the run fit and raises throughput, and the loss curve tracks the baseline step for step. Which explanation of that result is correct?
options: It tiles `Q`, `K` and `V` into on-chip SRAM blocks and accumulates an online (streaming) softmax, so the NÃ—N score matrix is never materialised in HBM; the attention computed is exact and the speedup comes from cutting memory traffic
It sparsifies attention by skipping key blocks whose scores fall below a threshold, trading a small accuracy loss for lower memory and FLOPs
It lowers the arithmetic complexity of attention from O(NÂ²·d) to O(N·d·log N) by replacing the matmul with a fast transform
It stores the score matrix in fp8 rather than fp16, quartering attention activation memory
mcq.rationale: FlashAttention is an IO-aware but mathematically exact reformulation: running softmax statistics let each output tile be finished from tiles of `K` and `V`, so peak memory drops from O(NÂ²) to O(N) and the kernel becomes HBM-bandwidth bound rather than bandwidth-starved. FLOP count is unchanged â€” matching loss curves are the tell that nothing was approximated.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses exact FlashAttention with block-sparse or approximate attention; an approximation would not reproduce the baseline loss curve
Assumes an IO-aware kernel must reduce arithmetic complexity, when it performs the same matmuls with better memory locality
Attributes the saving to lower precision rather than to never writing the score matrix to HBM at all

mcq.stem: To simplify a bidirectional transformer encoder used for sentence classification, a teammate deletes the positional encoding added to the token embeddings and changes nothing else. Training runs without error, but accuracy collapses on tasks that depend on word order. What is the underlying cause?
options: Without the positional encoding the residual stream loses its scale, so LayerNorm can no longer normalise activations correctly
The position-wise feed-forward blocks can no longer mix information across positions
Self-attention requires a fixed maximum length, so variable-length batches now interfere with one another
Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so with no positional signal the encoder produces the same representations for any reordering of the same tokens
mcq.rationale: Attention computes a weighted sum over a set of tokens; permuting the inputs simply permutes the outputs. Order information enters a transformer only through positional encodings (or a causal mask, absent in a bidirectional encoder), so removing them leaves the model with a bag of tokens.
misconceptions: Attributes the failure to activation scaling/normalisation rather than to lost order information
Believes the FFN mixes across positions; it is applied independently at each position and never carried order information
Confuses positional encodings with padding masks or a hard length constraint
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You reimplement multi-head attention and omit the `1 / sqrt(head_dim)` factor applied to the scores before `softmax`. With `head_dim = 128` the model trains far worse than the reference implementation, and logged attention weights are nearly one-hot from the very first step. What is the mechanism?
options: The unscaled logits overflow fp16, producing `inf` values so the softmax returns `NaN` and the updates are discarded

With roughly unit-variance `Q` and `K` entries the dot product has variance proportional to `head_dim`, so logits grow like `sqrt(head_dim)`; the softmax saturates and its Jacobian â€” and hence the gradient flowing into `Q` and `K` â€” becomes vanishingly small
Without the factor the attention weights no longer sum to 1, so each output stops being a convex combination of the value vectors
The factor exists to compensate for concatenating `n_heads` heads, so omitting it leaves the output projection's input `n_heads` times too large
mcq.rationale: A dot product of two `head_dim`-dimensional vectors with unit-variance components has variance `head_dim`, so raw logits sit on a `sqrt(head_dim)` scale â€” about 11 at `head_dim = 128`. Softmax over logits that spread that widely is essentially an argmax, and a saturated softmax has near-zero derivative, so the query and key projections receive almost no learning signal.
misconceptions: Confuses a gradient-scale problem with a numeric-range problem; logits of order `sqrt(128)` are nowhere near fp16 overflow, and the symptom is peaked weights, not `NaN`
CORRECT
Thinks the scale factor performs the normalisation; softmax normalises to 1 regardless of how the logits are scaled
Confuses per-head logit scaling with a normalisation of the head-concatenation, which is handled by the output projection

mcq.stem: A RoPE-based decoder pretrained with a 4k context degrades sharply when fed 16k-token inputs. You apply linear position interpolation â€” dividing every position index by 4 before computing the rotary embedding â€” then fine-tune briefly on long documents, and 16k quality recovers. What does the interpolation actually fix?
options: It keeps the rotary phase angles within the range seen during pretraining, so the model interpolates between relative-position patterns it has already learned instead of extrapolating into an unseen regime where attention logits behave erratically
It resizes the learned positional embedding table from 4k to 16k rows so that the additional positions have trained vectors
It rescales attention logits so the softmax does not grow over-diffuse as the number of attended tokens increases
It shrinks the KV cache by a factor of 4, which is what restores long-context quality
mcq.rationale: RoPE encodes relative position as a rotation whose angle is `position * frequency`. Beyond the pretraining length the low-frequency components reach angles the model never observed, and attention logits at those relative offsets are effectively untrained. Dividing positions by the extension factor compresses all angles back into the observed range, turning extrapolation into interpolation, which a short fine-tune can adapt to.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Treats RoPE as a learned absolute embedding table; RoPE applies a fixed rotation and has no trained position parameters to resize
Confuses position interpolation with length-dependent logit or temperature scaling; interpolation alters phase angles, not logit magnitude
Conflates a positional remapping with a memory optimisation; the KV cache size is unchanged and would not explain quality

mcq.stem: You build a linear probe: an ImageNet-pretrained `ResNet-50` is put in `.eval()` under `torch.no_grad()` to cache penultimate features, and a logistic-regression head is fitted on those cached vectors. Your dataloader applies only `ToTensor()`, so pixels arrive in `[0, 1]` with no channel mean/std normalisation. Compared with applying the pretraining normalisation, what should you expect?
options: No change, because the first `BatchNorm2d` layer standardises activations and absorbs any affine change to the input
No change, because the logistic-regression head is trained on whatever features it receives and will learn to compensate

Lower downstream accuracy, because the frozen stack's BatchNorm running statistics were estimated on normalised inputs, so activations are pushed off-distribution and nothing in the frozen graph can adapt
Slower convergence of the head only, because unnormalised inputs make the loss surface ill-conditioned; raising the head's learning rate restores the same accuracy
mcq.rationale: In `.eval()` mode BatchNorm applies fixed `running_mean`/`running_var` rather than re-standardising the current batch, so an input distribution shift propagates through the frozen convolutions instead of being cancelled. The features handed to the head are therefore computed in a regime the backbone never saw, and because the backbone is frozen there is no mechanism to recover. Using the checkpoint's own preprocessing (e.g. `weights.transforms()`) is the fix.
misconceptions: Believes eval-mode BatchNorm re-standardises per batch; it uses frozen running statistics and cannot absorb the shift
Treats the frozen backbone as invertible, as if a linear head could undo a shift that passed through many nonlinearities
CORRECT
Reframes a representation-quality problem as an optimisation-conditioning problem of the head

mcq.stem: You fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained `ResNet-50` on 2,000 histology images with `batch_size=8`. You freeze the backbone with `for p in backbone.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False`, pass only the new head's parameters to the optimiser, and call `model.train()` at the start of each epoch. Training loss falls smoothly, but validation accuracy oscillates between epochs and ends below a plain scikit-learn linear probe on cached features from the same checkpoint. What is the most likely cause?
options: `model.train()` leaves BatchNorm in training mode, so `running_mean`/`running_var` are buffers that keep updating from noisy batch-of-8 statistics even though the weights are frozen, drifting the eval-time features away from the pretrained ones
Passing frozen parameters through the optimiser lets weight decay keep shrinking the backbone weights each step, because decay is applied independently of the gradient
Dropout is still active in `model.train()`, injecting noise into the frozen features so the head fits a representation that differs from the one used at validation
A batch size of 8 makes the head's gradient estimate too noisy; accumulating gradients over several batches before `optimizer.step()` would remove the oscillation
mcq.rationale: `requires_grad = False` only stops gradients reaching learnable parameters. BatchNorm's running statistics are non-learnable buffers updated in the forward pass whenever the module is in training mode, so every epoch overwrites the pretrained statistics with estimates from 8 in-domain images. Validation runs in `.eval()` mode against those corrupted buffers, which is why held-out accuracy moves while training loss looks healthy. Calling `.eval()` on the BatchNorm modules after `model.train()` (or freezing them via `module.track_running_stats = False`) restores parity with the cached-feature probe.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Believes decoupled weight decay updates parameters with no gradient; PyTorch optimisers skip parameters whose `.grad` is `None`
Attributes the train/eval discrepancy to dropout, which torchvision's `ResNet-50` does not use and which leaves no persistent state
Blames stochastic gradient noise in the head, which would not produce features that differ between training and evaluation passes

mcq.stem: You wrap a single `model(x)` forward pass on CUDA tensors between two `time.perf_counter()` calls and measure 0.4 ms â€” far less than the kernels could possibly take for this model. What explains the number, and what makes the measurement trustworthy?
options: `time.perf_counter()` lacks the resolution needed for GPU work; only `torch.cuda.Event` timers can resolve sub-millisecond kernels
The model was still in `train()` mode, so autograd recorded the graph lazily and deferred the real compute until `backward()`
CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous, so the host timer stops while the GPU is still working; call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before the second timestamp, after a few warm-up iterations
cuDNN served the call from its autotuning cache, returning the previously computed output instead of re-running the convolutions
mcq.rationale: CUDA is asynchronous: `model(x)` returns as soon as the kernels are enqueued on the stream, so a host-side clock measures launch overhead rather than execution. `torch.cuda.synchronize()` (or CUDA events recorded on the stream) forces the host to wait for the queue to drain. Warm-up iterations also absorb one-off costs such as cuDNN algorithm selection and caching-allocator growth, which otherwise land in the first measured pass.
misconceptions: Blames clock resolution; `perf_counter()` is nanosecond-resolution â€” the problem is what is being timed, not the timer
Believes the forward pass is deferred until `backward()`; PyTorch eager mode executes forward ops immediately
CORRECT
Confuses cuDNN benchmark autotuning, which caches an algorithm choice, with caching and reusing the output tensor

mcq.stem: A `DistributedDataParallel` job trains correctly on one GPU but hangs silently at `loss.backward()` on 4 GPUs whenever a data-dependent branch in `forward()` skips an auxiliary head on some ranks. What is the mechanism behind the hang?
options: DDP attaches an autograd hook to every parameter and all-reduces a gradient bucket only once all of that bucket's parameters have produced gradients; parameters the branch skipped never fire, so the bucket's collective is never launched while other ranks wait inside theirs
NCCL requires every rank to present identically shaped tensors, and skipping the auxiliary head changes the shape of the loss tensor on the affected ranks
The skipped head's gradients are `None`, and NCCL blocks indefinitely rather than erroring when handed a null buffer
With the default `gradient_as_bucket_view=False`, gradients are copied into a flat buffer, and the copy blocks until every module has written its slice
mcq.rationale: At construction DDP partitions parameters into gradient buckets and registers a per-parameter autograd hook. A bucket's all-reduce fires only when every parameter in it has produced a gradient. If a branch bypasses a submodule on one rank, those parameters get no gradient, that bucket never becomes ready, and ranks that did enter the collective block forever â€” a collective mismatch, not a crash. `find_unused_parameters=True` makes DDP walk the autograd graph each iteration and mark the missing parameters ready, at the cost of that traversal.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Attributes the deadlock to tensor-shape mismatch rather than to per-parameter reduction-readiness bookkeeping
Assumes the collective runs with a null buffer; the all-reduce for that bucket is never launched at all
Confuses a memory-layout option for gradient buckets with the readiness tracking that actually stalls the collective

mcq.stem: A training script calls `model.to(device)` on one line and `batch.to(device)` on the next, then raises `RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device`. Which line failed to do what the author intended, and why?
options: `model.to(device)` moves only buffers such as BatchNorm running statistics; the parameters stay on the CPU until the first backward pass
`nn.Module.to()` moves parameters and buffers in place, but `Tensor.to()` returns a new tensor and leaves the original where it was â€” `batch` must be reassigned
Both calls are in place; the failure comes from the optimizer, which must be reconstructed after the model changes device
Both calls are lazy and only take effect at the next `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, which the script never reaches
mcq.rationale: `nn.Module.to()` mutates the module â€” it moves parameters and buffers and returns `self`, so discarding the return value is harmless. `Tensor.to()` is functional: it returns a copy on the target device and leaves the source tensor untouched. The batch therefore remains on the CPU unless the result is bound back, as in `batch = batch.to(device)`.
misconceptions: Wrongly believes `Module.to()` is partial; it relocates parameters and buffers alike
CORRECT
Confuses the tensor/module asymmetry with the separate question of optimizer construction order
Invents lazy device-transfer semantics; the real asymmetry is in-place versus returning a new tensor

mcq.stem: Before spending GPU-hours on a full run, you want the single cheapest diagnostic that will expose a wiring bug anywhere in the model, loss, or optimizer step â€” a wrong loss reduction, a `detach()` that cuts the graph, an optimizer that is never stepped, or labels misaligned with inputs. Which check exercises all of those at once?
options: Confirm the loss at initialisation is close to `-log(1/C)` for a `C`-class problem
Enable `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)` for one epoch and inspect the reported trace
Compare the first epoch's training curve against a linear baseline on the same features
Train on one fixed mini-batch for a few hundred steps and confirm the loss drives to near zero
mcq.rationale: If the forward pass, loss reduction, backward pass, and optimizer step are genuinely connected, a network with adequate capacity must memorise a handful of examples and push the loss to ~0. A loss that plateaus on a single batch localises the fault to the loop itself â€” a detached graph, a zero learning rate, a missing `optimizer.step()`, an unzeroed gradient, or targets that do not correspond to the inputs â€” before any data or generalisation question arises.
misconceptions: A correct initial loss validates the output head's scale but says nothing about whether gradients flow or the optimizer actually updates weights
Anomaly mode surfaces ops that produce NaN/inf; it stays silent on a detached graph or swapped labels that train smoothly to the wrong target
Measures predictive quality rather than whether the training loop is correctly wired
CORRECT

mcq.stem: A mixed-precision loop calls `scaler.scale(loss).backward()`, then `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)`, then `scaler.step(optimizer)` and `scaler.update()`. Training is unstable and the returned pre-clip gradient norm is in the tens of thousands on every step. What is wrong?
options: `clip_grad_norm_` must be called before `backward()` so autograd can enforce the bound as gradients are produced
At clip time the gradients still carry the scaler's multiplier, so the norm is measured in scaled units; `scaler.unscale_(optimizer)` must run first
`GradScaler` already clips internally, so the explicit call clips a second time and collapses the effective step size
The threshold applies to `scaler.scale(loss)` rather than to the parameters, since the loss is what carries the scale factor
mcq.rationale: `GradScaler` multiplies the loss by a large dynamic factor so fp16 gradients do not underflow, and that factor is still present in every `param.grad` immediately after `backward()`. Clipping there compares an inflated norm against 1.0, so the clip binds on every step and rescales gradients by a ratio that shifts whenever the scale factor is adjusted â€” an effective learning rate that jumps around. `scaler.unscale_(optimizer)` divides the gradients back in place first; `scaler.step()` then detects they are already unscaled and skips its own unscale before checking for inf/NaN.
misconceptions: Misorders the schedule; clipping operates on `.grad` tensors, which exist only after `backward()` has run
CORRECT
Believes `GradScaler` clips; it only scales, inspects gradients for inf/NaN, and adapts the scale factor
Confuses loss scaling with gradient clipping; the norm threshold applies to gradients, not to the loss value

mcq.stem: Under `DistributedDataParallel` you accumulate gradients over 8 micro-batches before each `optimizer.step()`, calling `loss.backward()` on every micro-batch. Profiling shows roughly 8Ã— the NCCL all-reduce traffic of a non-accumulating run at the same effective batch size. Which change removes the redundant communication while producing mathematically identical gradients?
options: Divide each micro-batch loss by 8 before `backward()`, so the repeated all-reduces average to the same value and NCCL coalesces them
Wrap the first 7 micro-batches in `torch.no_grad()` so only the final one produces gradients that need reducing
Set `gradient_as_bucket_view=True`, which lets DDP reuse a single flat buffer and issue one all-reduce per accumulation window
Run the first 7 micro-batches inside the `model.no_sync()` context and the 8th outside it, letting gradients accumulate locally before one collective reduces the full sum
mcq.rationale: DDP launches a bucket all-reduce from the autograd hooks of every `backward()`, so naive accumulation pays a full synchronisation per micro-batch. `model.no_sync()` suppresses that reduction for its enclosing block while gradients still accumulate into `.grad` locally. Because all-reduce is linear, reducing the summed local gradients once â€” on the final micro-batch, run outside the context â€” yields exactly what per-micro-batch synchronisation would have produced, at one eighth of the traffic.
misconceptions: Corrects the loss scaling but not the communication pattern; DDP still fires a bucket all-reduce on every `backward()`
`no_grad()` discards the gradients of 7 of the 8 micro-batches rather than merely deferring their synchronisation
Confuses a gradient-memory layout optimisation with control over when collectives are launched; bucket views change neither the count nor the timing of all-reduces
CORRECT

mcq.stem: A DDP training loop constructs `DataLoader(dataset, sampler=DistributedSampler(dataset, shuffle=True))` once and never touches the sampler again. What happens to the data ordering across epochs?
options: Every epoch replays the identical permutation and the identical rank-to-shard assignment, because the shuffle is seeded from an epoch counter that is only advanced by `set_epoch()`
Each rank draws its own independent permutation per epoch, so ranks overlap and some examples are processed twice within an epoch
The sampler silently falls back to sequential order, because `shuffle=True` is honoured only when `num_replicas` is passed explicitly
The `DataLoader` reshuffles on each `__iter__()` regardless of the sampler, so the behaviour is already correct
mcq.rationale: `DistributedSampler` derives its permutation deterministically from `seed + epoch` so that all ranks compute the same ordering and then take disjoint slices of it. The `epoch` attribute changes only when you call `sampler.set_epoch(epoch)` at the top of each epoch. Left at 0, the permutation is fixed for the whole run, so each rank repeatedly sees the same fixed subset in the same order â€” which removes the shuffling that SGD relies on and measurably degrades convergence.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes independent per-rank seeding; the shared seed is precisely what lets ranks partition one permutation without overlap
Invents a dependency on `num_replicas`, which defaults to the world size read from the initialised process group
Believes the loader shuffles anyway; supplying a sampler is mutually exclusive with `shuffle=True` on the `DataLoader`

mcq.stem: Training at batch size 32 fits comfortably in GPU memory, but the validation loop at the same batch size raises `CUDA out of memory` within a few batches. What is the most likely cause?
options: The validation split is transferred to the GPU in full before iteration starts
`model.eval()` was not called, so dropout masks are materialised for every layer
The forward pass runs without `torch.no_grad()`, so autograd keeps intermediate activations alive for a backward pass that never happens
The optimizer's momentum buffers are allocated lazily and first appear when validation begins
mcq.rationale: Autograd retains every intermediate activation so gradients can be computed later. During training that memory is released once `backward()` runs; in an evaluation loop nothing ever calls `backward()`, so the whole graph stays resident for the batch â€” and any accumulation such as `total_loss += loss` keeps it alive across batches. Wrapping the loop in `torch.no_grad()` (or `torch.inference_mode()`) stops the graph being recorded at all, cutting peak memory to roughly one layer's activations at a time.
misconceptions: Confuses a `DataLoader`'s lazy per-batch transfer with bulk preloading of the split
`eval()` changes dropout and BatchNorm behaviour; dropout masks are a small fraction of the retained activation graph
CORRECT
Optimizer state is allocated on the first `optimizer.step()`, during training, not during evaluation

mcq.stem: Your PyTorch validation loop wraps the forward pass in `with torch.no_grad():` but never calls `model.eval()`. The network contains `nn.BatchNorm2d` and `nn.Dropout` layers. What actually happens to those layers and to the model's running statistics during validation?
options: Nothing changes â€” `torch.no_grad()` already puts the network into inference mode, so BatchNorm and Dropout behave exactly as they would after `model.eval()`
Only Dropout is affected; BatchNorm normalises with its stored `running_mean`/`running_var` in both modes, so the metric stays stable

BatchNorm normalises each validation batch with that batch's own statistics and updates its running estimates from validation data, and Dropout keeps zeroing activations, so the score varies with batch composition and the running stats are contaminated
