The forward pass also updates the weights, because train mode keeps gradient tracking and the optimiser step live
mcq.rationale: `torch.no_grad()` only stops autograd from recording the graph; it does not touch each module's `training` flag. With that flag still `True`, `BatchNorm2d` normalises using the current mini-batch mean/variance and folds them into `running_mean`/`running_var` (so the val data leaks into the statistics used later), and `Dropout` continues to zero activations. The reported metric therefore depends on how examples happen to be grouped into batches and is typically noisy and pessimistic.
misconceptions: Conflates disabling gradient tracking with switching layer behaviour; `no_grad()` never flips the `training` flag
Believes BatchNorm always reads its running estimates, missing the batch-statistics path taken in train mode
CORRECT
Thinks a forward pass alone mutates parameters; updates need a `backward()` plus `optimizer.step()`

mcq.stem: An image classifier reaches 92% top-1 on your test set, but its reliability diagram shows mean confidence far above accuracy in every bin, and a downstream router that auto-accepts any prediction above `0.9` softmax confidence is letting too many errors through. You fit a single scalar temperature `T` on a held-out calibration split by minimising NLL over `softmax(logits / T)`, then divide logits by that `T` at inference. What is the effect on top-1 accuracy and on expected calibration error (ECE)?
options: Top-1 accuracy is unchanged because dividing every logit by the same positive scalar preserves their ordering; only the softmax sharpness moves, so ECE and NLL fall
Accuracy drops a point or two as the decision boundary shifts toward the majority class, which is the price paid for the lower ECE
Both improve, because the fitted temperature re-ranks the class scores toward the classes the calibration split favours
Neither changes on the test set â€” a temperature fitted on a calibration split only calibrates that split, so it must be refitted on the test logits
mcq.rationale: Temperature scaling is a monotone rescaling applied identically to all logits of an example, so `argmax` is invariant and top-1 (and top-k ordering) cannot change. What it does change is the spread of the logits: with `T > 1` the softmax softens, so predicted confidences drop toward observed accuracy, reducing NLL and ECE. That is exactly what a router thresholding on confidence needs.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses a uniform monotone rescaling with a class-dependent bias or threshold shift
Misses that a single positive scalar divisor cannot reorder logits, so no re-ranking is possible
Treats calibration as split-specific and would fit `T` on the test logits, leaking the evaluation set and destroying the held-out estimate

mcq.stem: You apply unstructured magnitude pruning to zero 50% of a CNN's weights and verify the sparsity, yet inference latency on your GPU is unchanged from the dense model. What explains the missing speedup?
options: The pruned weights are silently restored on the next forward pass, because magnitude pruning only masks weights during backpropagation
At 50% sparsity you are below the roughly 90% level at which sparse execution engages, and no GPU accelerates sparsity beneath that point

Unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights without shrinking the tensor's dense shape, so a standard dense `GEMM` still runs the full multiply-accumulate unless sparse kernels or hardware exploit the zeros
The GPU already skips zero-valued multiply-accumulates, so the compute saving exists but is masked by a memory-bandwidth bottleneck
mcq.rationale: Zeroing scattered weights leaves the weight tensor the same size, and dense `GEMM` kernels multiply every element regardless of value. Real speedups need structured pruning (removing whole channels or filters) that shrinks the tensors, or sparse kernels/hardware such as 2:4 sparsity that actually skip the zeros.
misconceptions: Treats pruning as a temporary training-time mask rather than a permanent zeroing that persists at inference
Invents a universal sparsity threshold below which no hardware can accelerate sparse models
CORRECT
Assumes general dense matrix-multiply hardware dynamically skips zero operands, which it does not

mcq.stem: You quantise a 7B-parameter LLM to 4-bit weight-only with `GPTQ` and serve single-request autoregressive decoding on one GPU; each layer dequantises its weights to `FP16` before the matmul. Token-generation latency still drops versus the `FP16` model despite the added dequantisation work. Why?
options: Single-sequence decoding is memory-bandwidth bound -- every generated token must stream all weights from HBM -- so loading 4-bit rather than 16-bit weights cuts the dominant cost even though the matmul itself runs in `FP16`
The matmul executes directly on the GPU's `INT4` tensor cores, roughly quadrupling arithmetic throughput per layer
`GPTQ` prunes redundant attention heads during its calibration pass, so there is less compute per token
Dequantisation is effectively free because it overlaps with attention's softmax, leaving throughput bounded only by the KV-cache size
mcq.rationale: At batch size 1, decoding is dominated by reading weights out of HBM, not by arithmetic. 4-bit weights quarter that memory traffic, so latency falls even though the product is computed in `FP16` after an on-the-fly dequantise. The gain largely disappears in compute-bound regimes such as large-batch prefill.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes weight-only quantisation performs `INT4` arithmetic; the weights are dequantised and the matmul runs in `FP16`
Confuses quantisation with pruning -- `GPTQ` rounds weights and removes no heads
Misattributes the speedup to dequant/softmax overlap and KV-cache size rather than reduced weight-memory traffic

mcq.stem: Running inference in `FP16`, some activations overflow to `inf`; switching to `BF16` at the same 16 bits eliminates the overflow. Which property of `BF16` is responsible?
options: `BF16` doubles the mantissa width of `FP16`, so rounding error shrinks and partial sums stop overflowing
`BF16` keeps `FP32`'s 8-bit exponent, so it spans the same dynamic range as `FP32` and represents magnitudes that overflow `FP16`'s 5-bit exponent -- at the cost of fewer mantissa bits
`BF16` stores values as two's-complement integers, a format that saturates instead of overflowing to `inf`
`BF16` applies an automatic loss-scaling factor that shifts activations back into the representable range
mcq.rationale: `BF16` and `FP16` are both 16 bits, but `BF16` allocates 8 bits to the exponent (matching `FP32`) and only 7 to the mantissa, whereas `FP16` uses a 5-bit exponent with a maximum finite value near 65504. The wider exponent gives `BF16` `FP32`-like range, avoiding overflow while trading away precision.
misconceptions: Frames overflow as a precision problem and wrongly believes `BF16` has more mantissa bits than `FP16`, when it has fewer
CORRECT
Believes `BF16` is an integer format rather than a floating-point one with a wide exponent
Confuses the `BF16` format with `FP16` loss-scaling, which is a separate training technique

mcq.stem: Distilling a large teacher into a smaller student, you train the student against the teacher's temperature-softened output distribution rather than only the one-hot ground-truth labels. What does this soft-target signal add that hard labels cannot?
options: It filters mislabelled examples, so the student never fits the noise present in the original labels
The temperature term enlarges the logits, which raises the student's effective learning rate and speeds convergence
It lets the student read the teacher's output at inference and drop its own softmax head, cutting parameters
The probabilities the teacher assigns to the non-target classes encode inter-class similarity ('dark knowledge'), giving each example a richer, lower-variance training signal than a one-hot label
mcq.rationale: A one-hot label says only which class is correct. The teacher's full softened distribution reveals how it rates the wrong classes -- which errors are near-misses -- and that structure transfers information a hard label omits, letting a smaller student learn effectively from fewer examples.
misconceptions: Mistakes distillation for label denoising; soft targets can carry the teacher's mistakes rather than remove them
Misreads temperature: dividing logits by `T > 1` softens (shrinks) the distribution and is not a learning-rate control
Thinks the student consumes teacher logits at run time; the student trains against them but serves standalone with its own head
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Quantising a >6B-parameter transformer's activations to `INT8` with a single per-tensor scale collapses accuracy, though the identical scheme was fine on smaller models. What is the established cause?
options: `INT8` is unsigned, so the negative half of each post-`GELU` activation wraps around to large positive codes
Deeper models accumulate quantisation error multiplicatively layer over layer until it saturates the `INT8` range

A few hidden dimensions carry systematic large-magnitude outliers; a per-tensor scale stretched to cover them maps the remaining values onto only a handful of `INT8` levels, destroying their resolution
The embedding matrix dominates the parameter budget, so its rounding error propagates into every downstream token representation
mcq.rationale: Above roughly 6.7B parameters, transformers develop a small set of outlier feature dimensions with far larger activation magnitudes. A per-tensor scale must span those outliers, so ordinary activations collapse onto a few quantisation levels. Fixes keep those dimensions in higher precision (`LLM.int8()`) or migrate the range from activations into weights (`SmoothQuant`).
misconceptions: Believes `INT8` is unsigned; signed `INT8` represents negatives, and the failure is outliers, not sign
Attributes the collapse to depth-wise error compounding rather than emergent per-dimension activation outliers
CORRECT
Confuses parameter count with the activation-range problem; embeddings are not the source of the error

mcq.stem: You fine-tune a transformer whose tokenizer uses byte-level BPE (as in GPT-2 and RoBERTa). A user submits the never-before-seen product code `Xyzzy-9000`. How does the tokenizer represent it?
options: It emits a single `[UNK]` token, because the code is absent from the vocabulary
It raises an error until `Xyzzy-9000` is added to the vocabulary and the embeddings are resized
It decomposes the string into several subword/byte tokens, so any input is representable without an `[UNK]`
It switches to one token per Unicode character for this word only
mcq.rationale: Byte-level BPE builds its merges over the 256 possible byte values, so every UTF-8 string decomposes into known byte units plus learned merges. There is no out-of-vocabulary case and therefore no `[UNK]` token.
misconceptions: Applies word-level vocabulary semantics, where an unseen word maps to `[UNK]`
Assumes tokenisation rejects unfamiliar input instead of decomposing it into subunits
CORRECT
Confuses byte-level fallback with per-Unicode-character tokenisation

mcq.stem: You are training a token-classification (NER) model with a WordPiece tokenizer that splits `Nakamoto` into `Naka`, `##mo`, `##to`, while your gold data has one label per word. Following the standard HuggingFace alignment convention, how are the three subword tokens labelled for the loss?
options: The first subword receives the word's label and the remaining subwords are set to `-100` so they are ignored by the loss
All three subwords receive the word's label so each contributes equally to the loss
Only the final subword is labelled, because `##` marks it as the continuation that carries the word
The extra subwords are dropped so the sequence keeps exactly one token per word
mcq.rationale: The convention tags the first subword with the word's label and sets the rest to `-100`, the cross-entropy ignore index, so continuation pieces do not contribute to the loss while the full token sequence still feeds the encoder.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Over-weights multi-subword words by treating every piece as an independent labelled example
Misreads the `##` continuation marker as flagging the semantically primary token
Assumes subwords can be dropped without breaking token-to-hidden-state alignment

mcq.stem: In NLTK, `WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize('better')` returns `'better'`, but `WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize('better', pos='a')` returns `'good'`. What does this behaviour demonstrate?
options: Lemmatisation is non-deterministic and may return different lemmas on repeated calls
The lemmatizer is faulty, since `'better'` should always reduce to `'good'`
Adjective lemmas are only available through the Snowball stemmer, not WordNet
Lemmatisation is part-of-speech dependent; with no POS supplied the lemmatizer assumes a noun and leaves many words unchanged
mcq.rationale: The WordNet lemmatizer maps a token to a dictionary form using its part of speech; its default POS is noun, so `'better'` only reduces to `'good'` once it is told the word is an adjective (`pos='a'`).
misconceptions: Mistakes a POS-dependent mapping for nondeterministic behaviour
Treats a documented POS requirement as a bug
Confuses WordNet lemmatisation with rule-based suffix-stripping stemmers
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Two records both display as `cafÃ©`, yet `record_a == record_b` is `False` and they hash differently: one stores `Ã©` as a single precomposed code point, the other as `e` followed by a combining acute accent. Which preprocessing step makes them compare equal?
options: Lowercasing both strings with `.lower()`
Applying Unicode normalisation such as `unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s)` to both strings
Stripping leading and trailing whitespace with `.strip()`
Encoding both to ASCII with `errors='ignore'` to drop the accent
mcq.rationale: The strings differ only in Unicode composition â€” one precomposed code point versus a base letter plus a combining mark. Normalising both to the same form (NFC or NFD) yields identical code-point sequences that compare and hash equally.
misconceptions: Confuses case normalisation with normalising a character's code-point composition
CORRECT
Confuses whitespace trimming with code-point composition
Assumes lossy ASCII folding is equivalent to Unicode normalisation

mcq.stem: A teammate puts a bag-of-words cleaning pipeline â€” lowercasing, stripping all punctuation, and removing stopwords â€” in front of a pretrained `bert-base-cased` model, and downstream accuracy drops versus feeding lightly-cleaned text. Why does cleaning that helped a TF-IDF classifier hurt the transformer?
options: Transformers require the raw bytes and cannot accept any string preprocessing at all
The cleaning shrinks the vocabulary below the model's minimum embedding count
The model was pretrained on natural text, so its subword tokenizer and learned representations rely on the casing, punctuation, and function words that the cleaning removes
Stopword removal changes the detected language, so the tokenizer routes text to the wrong embedding matrix
mcq.rationale: A pretrained transformer expects inputs from the same distribution as its pretraining corpus; its subword tokenizer and contextual embeddings encode case, punctuation, and function words as signal. Aggressive normalisation built for sparse bag-of-words features discards that information and creates a train/serve mismatch.
misconceptions: Overstates the point into a false absolute; light, distribution-preserving cleaning is fine
Invents a vocabulary-size floor unrelated to how embeddings work
CORRECT
Fabricates a language-routing mechanism the tokenizer does not have

mcq.stem: In a BM25 keyword index you swap lemmatisation for the aggressive Lancaster stemmer. Recall for morphological variants improves, but querying `university` now also returns documents about `universe` and `universal`. What is the mechanism and its standard name?
options: Under-stemming: the stemmer left distinct roots intact, so related terms were indexed separately
Over-stemming: the stemmer collapsed words with different meanings to a shared stem (e.g. `univers`), conflating them in the index and lowering precision
Lemma drift: the Lancaster lemmatizer picked the wrong dictionary lemma because it lacked POS tags
Index corruption: aggressive stemming exceeds the analyzer's token-length limit and truncates terms
mcq.rationale: Aggressive stemmers strip suffixes so eagerly that words with different meanings but similar surface forms reduce to one stem, merging distinct concepts into a single index term. This over-stemming raises recall at the cost of precision; the opposite failure, under-stemming, leaves related forms unmerged.
misconceptions: Inverts the definitions of over- and under-stemming
CORRECT
Miscasts a rule-based stemmer as a POS-dependent lemmatizer and invents 'lemma drift'
Attributes a precision problem to an unrelated token-length/truncation limit

mcq.stem: You fit a `TfidfVectorizer` on your training corpus, then call `.transform()` on live production text. A slang token that never appeared in training now occurs frequently in the incoming text. How does `transform` represent that token in the output vectors?
options: It is added to the vocabulary on the fly, increasing the output's dimensionality
It raises a dimension-mismatch error, since the feature count no longer matches `fit`
It is silently dropped and contributes nothing, because `transform` projects onto the vocabulary and IDF weights frozen during `fit`
It is routed to a reserved `<UNK>` feature that `TfidfVectorizer` maintains for unseen tokens
mcq.rationale: `fit` freezes the vocabulary and IDF weights; `transform` only projects text onto those fixed columns. A token with no column is discarded -- `TfidfVectorizer` has no `<UNK>` bucket and never changes its feature dimension at transform time.
misconceptions: Assumes `transform` re-learns the vocabulary; only `fit`/`fit_transform` adds new terms
Expects a shape error, but unknown tokens are dropped and the feature dimension is fixed at `fit`
CORRECT
Invents an `<UNK>` bucket; `TfidfVectorizer` keeps no out-of-vocabulary feature

mcq.stem: You need sentence embeddings for semantic-similarity search. A teammate runs sentences through an off-the-shelf pretrained BERT (no further training), takes the raw `[CLS]` vector as each sentence's embedding, and ranks by cosine similarity -- but the rankings are poor. What is the primary reason?
options: Vanilla BERT was never trained so that cosine distance between `[CLS]` vectors reflects sentence meaning; models like Sentence-BERT fine-tune with a similarity objective to induce that geometry
The `[CLS]` token must be excluded and the remaining token vectors mean-pooled, which by itself yields calibrated similarities
BERT's vectors are too low-dimensional to separate sentences; projecting them to a higher dimension restores the similarities
Cosine similarity is undefined for transformer outputs; only Euclidean distance is meaningful for them
mcq.rationale: BERT's pretraining (masked-language modeling plus next-sentence prediction) optimises token prediction, not a space where cosine distance tracks sentence meaning, and the raw space is anisotropic. Sentence-BERT fine-tunes a siamese network on NLI/STS data so cosine similarity aligns with semantic similarity.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Attributes the failure to pooling; mean-pooled vanilla BERT is also weakly calibrated without a similarity-tuned objective
Blames vector dimensionality rather than the pretraining objective and the anisotropic embedding geometry
Believes cosine is inapplicable to transformer embeddings; Sentence-BERT ranks precisely by cosine

mcq.stem: A plain bag-of-words model encodes the sentences `the cat chased the dog` and `the dog chased the cat`. How do the two resulting count vectors compare?
options: Different -- reversing the word order changes each token's count
Orthogonal -- the sentences carry opposite meaning, so their vectors are perpendicular
Different -- bag-of-words stores each token's position, which differs between the two
Identical -- bag-of-words records only token counts, and both sentences share the same counts
mcq.rationale: Bag-of-words maps a sentence to counts over the vocabulary. Both sentences share the multiset `{the:2, cat:1, chased:1, dog:1}`, so their vectors are identical; word order is discarded, which is exactly why the model cannot tell them apart.
misconceptions: Thinks counts depend on arrangement; the token multiset is identical either way
Conflates semantic opposition with vector geometry; bag-of-words encodes counts, not meaning
Believes bag-of-words records token positions; it stores only per-token frequencies
CORRECT

mcq.stem: In a static embedding model such as word2vec or GloVe, the token `bank` maps to one vector even though it means a riverbank in some sentences and a financial institution in others. What does this single-vector design imply, and how do contextual encoders differ?
options: Word2vec resolves the ambiguity at lookup time, returning the sense that matches each sentence
The one vector blends both senses into a single point; a contextual encoder like BERT instead produces a distinct vector per occurrence, conditioned on the surrounding tokens
The two senses are stored as separate rows and disambiguated by a part-of-speech tag
Contextual and static models behave the same here; each emits one vector per word type
mcq.rationale: A static model learns one vector per word type by averaging over all its contexts, so a polysemous token collapses its senses into a single point. A contextual encoder computes each token's vector from the whole sequence, so `bank` differs between `river bank` and `central bank`.
misconceptions: Thinks static lookup performs context-sensitive sense selection; it returns one fixed row per token
CORRECT
Imagines separate per-sense rows; a word type maps to exactly one static vector
Misses that per-occurrence contextualisation is what separates BERT-style encoders from static models

mcq.stem: You fine-tune a transformer to route support tickets, where one ticket can belong to several categories at once (for example both `billing` and `bug`). Which output-layer and loss configuration correctly models this multi-label setting?
options: A softmax over the categories with categorical cross-entropy, taking the arg-max category as the prediction
A softmax with categorical cross-entropy, then always emitting the top-2 categories by probability
An independent sigmoid on each category logit with binary cross-entropy, thresholding each output separately
A single softmax output trained with focal loss to handle the label overlap
mcq.rationale: Multi-label means each category is an independent yes/no decision, so each logit needs its own sigmoid trained with binary cross-entropy (Hugging Face's `multi_label_classification` problem type uses `BCEWithLogitsLoss`). A softmax normalises across categories so they compete and sum to 1, wrongly suppressing labels that genuinely co-occur.
misconceptions: Applies single-label multiclass (softmax normalisation) where labels co-occur, so competing categories are forced to suppress one another
Hard-codes a fixed count of labels per ticket instead of letting each label fire independently on its own threshold
CORRECT
Assumes focal loss removes softmax's mutual exclusivity; it reweights easy-versus-hard examples but still normalises across classes so labels keep competing

mcq.stem: You fine-tune BERT for token-level NER. WordPiece splits `Washington` into `Wash`, `##ing`, `##ton`, but your gold labels are one per word. Training uses `CrossEntropyLoss` with its default `ignore_index=-100`. What is the standard way to align the word's label to these subword tokens?
options: Label the first subword `Wash` with the word's tag and set `##ing` and `##ton` to `-100`, keeping them as context but excluding them from the loss
Copy the word's tag onto all three subwords so each one contributes a training signal
Drop `##ing` and `##ton` from the input so each word maps to exactly one token
Tag `##ing` and `##ton` as `O` so only the first subword carries the entity label
mcq.rationale: Setting continuation subwords to `-100` leaves them in the sequence so the model still attends to full-word context, while `CrossEntropyLoss` skips them, so one word is counted once. Copying the tag double-counts the word and can place several `B-` tags inside one span; dropping subwords desynchronises tokens from their contextual representations; tagging continuations `O` teaches the model that the interior of an entity is outside it.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Double-counts one word as several targets and can place multiple `B-` tags inside a single span, corrupting the BIO scheme
Removing continuation subwords breaks alignment with the model's contextual embeddings and destroys span boundaries
Labelling interior subwords `O` trains the model that the middle of an entity is outside any entity, fragmenting spans

mcq.stem: A binary spam classifier is evaluated on a corpus that is 98% `ham`. A trivial model that labels every email `ham` reaches 98% accuracy. Which metric exposes that this model is useless for catching spam?
options: Overall classification accuracy
Log-loss measured on the `ham` class only
The model's final training loss
Recall on the `spam` class
mcq.rationale: With a 98/2 split, accuracy is dominated by the majority class and stays high even when no spam is caught. Recall on `spam` is `TP / (TP + FN)`; the all-`ham` model has zero true positives, so its spam recall is 0, revealing the failure that accuracy hides.
misconceptions: Relies on the metric the imbalance already inflates; always predicting the majority is rewarded by accuracy
Scoring only the majority class measures what the model already gets right, not the spam it misses
Training loss reflects fit on the training set, not minority-class detection on the evaluation set
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You score an NER tagger with entity-level F1 as computed by `seqeval`. The gold labels are `[B-PER, I-PER]` over `Ada Lovelace`; your model predicts `[B-PER, O]`, tagging only `Ada`. How does entity-level scoring count this prediction?
options: As a partial match, giving half credit for the one overlapping token
As a false positive for the predicted `Ada` span and a false negative for the missed `Ada Lovelace` span, since the boundaries differ
As a true positive, because the entity type `PER` is correct
As a single false negative, leaving precision unaffected
mcq.rationale: Entity-level scoring compares whole spans, not tokens, and requires an exact match of both type and boundaries. The predicted `PER` span covers only `Ada`, matching no gold span, so it is a false positive, while the gold `Ada Lovelace` span goes unrecovered as a false negative. There is no partial credit, so both precision and recall drop.
misconceptions: Assumes span metrics give fractional credit for token overlap; CoNLL/`seqeval` scoring is exact-match only
CORRECT
Counts a correct type with wrong boundaries as a hit; entity-level matching needs both the type and the exact span to match
Remembers the missed gold entity but forgets that the wrong predicted span also counts against precision

mcq.stem: You are fine-tuning a BERT token-classification model for NER. Its WordPiece tokenizer splits `Washington` into `Wash` and `##ington`, so the special tokens `[CLS]`/`[SEP]` and every subword after the first are given the label `-100`. What does assigning `-100` accomplish during training?
options: It excludes those positions from the loss, because `-100` is the default `ignore_index` of PyTorch's cross-entropy loss
It assigns those positions the outside class `O`, so the model learns to predict them as non-entities
It signals the tokenizer to drop those pieces before the forward pass, shortening the sequence
It down-weights those positions so they contribute less to the loss without being fully excluded
mcq.rationale: PyTorch's cross-entropy loss ignores any position whose target equals `ignore_index` (default `-100`). Labelling special tokens and subword continuations `-100` trains the model on exactly one label per word while still feeding every subword through the encoder.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses the ignore sentinel with the `O` label; `O` is a real class the model predicts, whereas `-100` removes the position from the loss entirely
Thinks `-100` acts on tokenization; the subwords are still encoded and only the loss skips them
Reads `-100` as a soft down-weight rather than the hard exclusion enforced by `ignore_index`

mcq.stem: Your team bootstraps a relation-extraction training set by distant supervision: for every entity pair linked by `spouse` in Wikidata, you label all sentences mentioning both entities as expressing `spouse`. What is the principal risk this labelling scheme introduces?
options: It produces no usable labels, because Wikidata relations cannot be aligned to raw sentence text
False positives: many sentences mention both entities without asserting `spouse`, so the relation label is noisy
It guarantees precision, but recall collapses to only the entity pairs already stored in Wikidata
The model can only learn relations that are absent from the knowledge base
mcq.rationale: Distant supervision assumes co-occurrence implies the relation, which is too strong: two spouses are named together in many sentences that never state marriage, and those get mislabelled `spouse`. This false-positive noise is the classic weakness, mitigated by multi-instance ('at least one') formulations.
misconceptions: Misunderstands distant supervision, which aligns KB pairs to text by entity/string matching precisely to generate labels
CORRECT
Inverts the failure mode; distant supervision chiefly degrades precision through noisy positives rather than bounding recall this way
Reverses the mechanism; supervision comes from relations present in the KB, not those missing from it

mcq.stem: You are writing the span-decoding function that converts your NER model's per-token BIO tags into entity spans. For a two-token sequence tagged `B-PER B-PER`, how many entities should the function emit?
options: One two-token `PER` entity spanning both tokens
Zero, because `B-PER` may not immediately follow another `B-PER`
Two separate single-token `PER` entities, one per token
One `PER` entity whose right boundary is left uncertain
mcq.rationale: In BIO, every `B-` opens a new entity and only `I-` continues one. Two consecutive `B-PER` tags therefore mark two distinct one-token entities; a single two-token span would be tagged `B-PER I-PER`.
misconceptions: Thinks a multi-token span repeats `B-`; continuation is encoded with `I-PER`, not a second `B-PER`
Believes `B-` after `B-` is illegal; the sequence is valid and denotes two adjacent entities
CORRECT
Reads two adjacent entities as one span with a fuzzy boundary, which BIO does not encode

mcq.stem: Your information-extraction system runs NER first and feeds the predicted entity spans into a separate relation-classification model. Compared with a jointly trained entity-and-relation model, what is the characteristic weakness of this pipelined design?
options: It cannot use pretrained transformer encoders, since the two stages require incompatible tokenizers
Relation classification is intractable unless every sentence contains exactly two entities
It doubles the annotation budget, because both stages must be trained on identical labels
Cascading errors: an entity the NER stage misses or mis-bounds never reaches the relation stage, which cannot recover it
mcq.rationale: In a pipeline the relation model only sees NER's output, so any missed or wrongly delimited span is permanently lost to it. Joint models let relation signal inform entity decisions, reducing this error propagation.
misconceptions: Invents a tokenizer incompatibility; pipeline stages routinely share or independently apply transformer encoders
Fabricates a two-entity constraint; relation models score a variable number of candidate entity pairs per sentence
Confuses pipelining with annotation cost; the stages consume different label types, not doubled identical ones
CORRECT

mcq.stem: A document-level sentiment model labels the review `"The battery lasts all day, but the camera is unusable"` as `neutral`. Product managers need the sentiment toward *battery* and *camera* reported separately. Which approach directly produces that?
options: Raise the classifier's decision threshold so mixed reviews fall into `positive` or `negative` instead of `neutral`
Replace the softmax head with a regression head that emits one continuous polarity score per review
Run aspect-based sentiment analysis, extracting each aspect term and classifying polarity toward it individually
Oversample `neutral` reviews during training so the model learns to split them apart
mcq.rationale: A document-level model emits one label per review, so opposing polarities cancel into `neutral`. Aspect-based sentiment analysis extracts each aspect term (`battery`, `camera`) and assigns a polarity to each, which is exactly the per-aspect breakdown requested; threshold, regression-head, and resampling tweaks all still operate on a single review-level output.
misconceptions: Thinks shifting a decision threshold can recover per-aspect signal that a single document-level label has already collapsed
Believes one continuous review-level score can represent two opposing aspect polarities rather than averaging them out
CORRECT
Confuses a class-imbalance remedy with the need for aspect-level granularity

mcq.stem: You are sweeping the topic count `K` for an LDA model whose topics will be read and labelled by human analysts, and you will pick the `K` that optimises a single metric. Which selection criterion best serves interpretable topics?
options: Pick the `K` that maximises a topic-coherence score such as `c_v` or NPMI over each topic's top terms
Pick the `K` that minimises held-out perplexity, since a lower-perplexity model fits the data better
Pick the largest `K` your compute budget allows, because finer-grained topics are always more interpretable
Pick the `K` that maximises the average per-document topic entropy
mcq.rationale: Held-out perplexity measures predictive fit, which the 'reading tea leaves' result shows correlates weakly -- often negatively -- with how interpretable humans find the topics. Coherence metrics like `c_v` and NPMI score how often each topic's top words co-occur, tracking human judgements of topic quality far more reliably.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes lower held-out perplexity implies more interpretable topics, contrary to the documented anti-correlation between predictive fit and coherence
Conflates more topics with better topics, ignoring redundancy and fragmentation at large `K`
Mistakes a per-document topic-mixing statistic for a measure of within-topic word coherence

mcq.stem: Your team needs a first-pass sentiment signal on English tweets today. There is no labelled data and no time to train a model. Which option yields usable polarity scores out of the box?
options: Fine-tune `bert-base-uncased` on the tweets with a classification head
Train a logistic-regression classifier on TF-IDF features of the tweets
Train `word2vec` embeddings on the tweet corpus and read polarity from them
Apply a lexicon- and rule-based analyzer such as VADER, built for social-media text
mcq.rationale: VADER combines a sentiment lexicon with rules for negation, intensifiers, punctuation and emoji, so it returns `compound` polarity scores with no training and no labels -- a valid same-day baseline. Fine-tuning and TF-IDF classification both require labelled data, and `word2vec` produces embeddings, not sentiment.
misconceptions: Overlooks that fine-tuning requires labelled examples the team does not have
Forgets that supervised TF-IDF classification also needs labelled training data
Confuses distributional word embeddings with a ready-made sentiment signal
CORRECT

mcq.stem: After fitting LDA on a corpus of clinical notes, almost every topic's top words include `patient`, `history`, and `noted` -- terms that occur in nearly every document. What is the most effective fix?
options: Increase the number of training passes so the sampler separates the ubiquitous terms
Remove terms with very high document frequency (e.g. gensim `filter_extremes(no_above=0.5)`) and refit
Lower the concentration prior `alpha` so each document commits to fewer topics
Increase `K` so the ubiquitous terms spread across more topics
mcq.rationale: Terms present in nearly every document carry almost no discriminating signal yet have high raw counts, so LDA assigns them high probability across many topics' word distributions. Pruning these high-document-frequency terms (corpus-specific stopwords) removes the noise so the surviving words define distinct topics; more passes, prior tweaks, or a larger `K` leave the ubiquitous terms in place.
misconceptions: Treats a vocabulary/feature problem as a sampler-convergence problem
CORRECT
Targets document-topic sparsity, which does not stop a corpus-wide term from dominating each topic's word distribution
Assumes more topics dilute ubiquitous terms rather than replicating them across every topic

mcq.stem: You embed 2M catalogue descriptions with a `sentence-transformers` bi-encoder and index them; at query time you retrieve nearest neighbours by cosine similarity. A teammate wants to switch the metric to raw dot product for speed. Under what condition do dot product and cosine similarity rank the documents identically?
options: Always -- dot product and cosine similarity are the same operation, just written differently
When every embedding is mean-centred so each vector's components sum to zero
When all embeddings are L2-normalised to unit length, so the cosine denominator is always 1
Only when the queries and documents are produced by the same embedding model
mcq.rationale: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the two vectors' L2 norms. Normalising every embedding to unit length makes those norms 1, so cosine equals dot product and the two rank documents identically. Left unnormalised, longer document vectors earn inflated dot products and the two rankings can diverge.
misconceptions: Conflates the two metrics, ignoring that cosine divides out each vector's magnitude
Confuses mean-centring (which underlies Pearson correlation) with L2 normalisation
CORRECT
States a genuine requirement for meaningful retrieval, but not the condition that makes dot product equal cosine

mcq.stem: Your dense retriever returns the top-100 documents by cosine similarity, then a cross-encoder reranks them down to a final top-10. Both are transformer models, yet the cross-encoder reliably improves ranking quality. Which property of the cross-encoder explains the gain?
options: It encodes the query and each candidate document together in one pass, so self-attention models token-level interactions between them that independently computed embeddings cannot
It was trained on far more data, so it simply produces higher-quality embeddings than the bi-encoder
It compares longer embedding vectors under cosine similarity, capturing finer semantic distinctions
It caches document embeddings, letting it score the entire corpus rather than only a shortlist
mcq.rationale: A cross-encoder concatenates the query with a candidate document and runs full self-attention over the pair, emitting a single relevance score; query and document tokens attend to each other directly. A bi-encoder embeds each side independently into fixed vectors and can never model those cross-interactions. The price is that the cross-encoder cannot pre-compute document representations, so it is affordable only over a retrieved shortlist.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Attributes the gain to training-data volume rather than to the joint query-document encoding
Believes the cross-encoder outputs embeddings scored by cosine, when it emits a relevance score directly with no vector comparison
Reverses the caching property -- the bi-encoder pre-computes document vectors; the cross-encoder cannot, which is exactly why it is restricted to a shortlist

mcq.stem: A user searches your support portal for the exact Oracle error code `ORA-01555`. Your pure vector (dense) retriever returns semantically related troubleshooting pages but misses the page that literally contains that code. Which change most directly fixes this class of miss?
options: Increase the embedding dimensionality so rare tokens like the error code get their own dimensions
Lower the HNSW index's `ef_search` so the nearest-neighbour candidate set is tighter
Re-embed each page with a longer context window so the model sees more surrounding text
Add a BM25 lexical retriever (hybrid search), since exact term matching surfaces rare tokens that embeddings blur together
mcq.rationale: Dense embeddings capture meaning but smear rare, near-out-of-vocabulary strings such as error codes into nearby regions, so an exact identifier can be missed. BM25 scores documents on exact term overlap and reliably surfaces the page containing the literal token. Running both and fusing (hybrid retrieval) keeps semantic recall while restoring exact-match precision.
misconceptions: Assumes embedding dimensions map to individual tokens; they encode dense distributed features, not per-token slots
Confuses an ANN recall/speed parameter with the lexical-versus-semantic matching problem -- a tighter set would if anything drop more candidates
Thinks context-window length governs exact-term matching, which it does not
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You fine-tune a bi-encoder retriever with a contrastive InfoNCE objective using in-batch negatives. Empirically, raising the training batch size from 32 to 512 improves retrieval accuracy. What is the mechanism behind the improvement?
options: Larger batches lower the effective learning rate, which regularises the encoder and prevents overfitting
Each other example in the batch acts as a negative, so a larger batch gives more (and harder) negatives per positive, sharpening the contrastive signal
More examples per batch raise the embedding dimensionality, giving the model extra representational capacity
Bigger batches inflate the cosine-similarity scores, widening the margin between positives and negatives
mcq.rationale: With in-batch negatives, the other examples in the same batch serve as negatives for each query-positive pair. The InfoNCE softmax is normalised over those negatives, so a larger batch contrasts each positive against many more of them -- a closer approximation to normalising over the whole corpus -- producing a stronger gradient and a more discriminative embedding space. The lever is the number of negatives, not learning rate, dimensionality, or score scale.
misconceptions: Invents a batch-size/learning-rate coupling; batch size does not regularise the embedding space in this way
CORRECT
Confuses batch size with model width -- embedding dimension is fixed by the architecture, not by how many examples share a batch
Attributes the improvement to raw similarity magnitude rather than to the count of contrasted negatives

mcq.stem: Your Transformer encoder runs fine at 512 tokens but throws CUDA out-of-memory when you raise `max_length` to 2048 at inference, even though the model weights fit comfortably in GPU memory. Treating attention as standard (non-flash), how does the self-attention step scale with sequence length `n`, explaining the blow-up?
options: `O(n^2)`, since every token attends to every other, materialising an nÃ—n attention-score matrix
`O(n)`, since each token is processed once in a single forward pass
`O(n log n)`, from a tree-structured key lookup inside attention
`O(1)` in sequence length, since only network depth drives memory
mcq.rationale: Self-attention scores every pair of the `n` tokens, materialising an nÃ—n matrix whose compute and memory both grow with nÂ². Going from 512 to 2048 is a 4x length increase and roughly a 16x increase in attention memory, so activations OOM while the fixed-size weights still fit.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Mistakes attention for one independent pass per token, ignoring the all-pairs score matrix
Invents a log-linear attention cost; standard attention performs no sorted or tree-structured lookup
Confuses sequence-length scaling with model-depth scaling

mcq.stem: Two abstractive summarisation checkpoints score almost identically on ROUGE-L against your reference summaries, yet reviewers flag checkpoint B for stating revenue figures that never appear in the source article. What does this reveal about ROUGE-L as the metric for choosing between them?
options: It rewards longer summaries, so B is probably just producing more text than A
It scores subsequence overlap against the reference and never reads the source, so it cannot flag facts the article does not contain
It already captures factual consistency, so the human flags are most likely rater noise
It penalises paraphrase, so B was correctly marked down for rewording the source
mcq.rationale: ROUGE-L measures the longest common subsequence between the candidate and a reference summary; it compares surface tokens to that reference and never consults the source document. A fluent summary that fabricates figures can overlap the reference just as well as a faithful one, so catching unsupported claims needs a separate faithfulness or factual-consistency check.
misconceptions: Attributes the tie to length; ROUGE-L rewards subsequence overlap, not raw output length
CORRECT
Assumes ROUGE tracks factual consistency, so equal scores must mean equal faithfulness
Believes ROUGE penalises paraphrase; it cannot separate faithful rewording from fabrication

mcq.stem: In an extractive question-answering model (SQuAD-style, e.g. a fine-tuned BERT), how does the model produce the answer to a question given a context passage?
options: It generates the answer token-by-token from its full vocabulary, like a decoder language model
It retrieves the most semantically similar stored sentence from a vector index
It predicts a start-token index and an end-token index over the passage and returns the span between them
It classifies the question into one of a fixed, predefined set of answer labels
mcq.rationale: An extractive QA head places two linear classifiers over the encoder outputs, producing a start logit and an end logit for every context token; the answer is the contiguous span from the best start position to the best end position. Nothing is generated â€” the answer is always a substring of the supplied passage.
misconceptions: Confuses extractive span prediction with generative (abstractive) decoding
Confuses the reader model with a separate retriever/embedding-search step
CORRECT
Confuses open-vocabulary span extraction with fixed-label classification

mcq.stem: You score an NMT system with corpus BLEU, which multiplies a modified n-gram precision by a brevity penalty. What failure mode does the brevity-penalty term specifically guard against?
options: Over-long translations that pad the output with repeated n-grams
Translations that reorder words relative to the reference word order
Translations that rely on rare vocabulary absent from the reference
Very short translations, which can otherwise post high modified n-gram precision on a few confident words
mcq.rationale: BLEU has no recall term, so a very short candidate can achieve high modified n-gram precision by emitting only the few words it is most confident about. The brevity penalty scales the score down whenever the candidate is shorter than the reference, removing the incentive to translate too little.
misconceptions: Thinks the brevity penalty targets over-long output; shrinking long output would be a length penalty, not BLEU's brevity term
Confuses precision-based BLEU with a word-order or reordering penalty
Confuses vocabulary rarity with the length-based brevity penalty
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Your extractive QA pipeline handles passages longer than the model's `max_seq_length` by splitting each into overlapping windows controlled by `doc_stride`. Why is the overlap between consecutive windows necessary?
options: It raises the effective batch size, speeding up inference over long documents
It ensures an answer span that a non-overlapping split would cut in two still appears intact within at least one window
It deduplicates repeated passages so each sentence is scored only once
It is required for the softmax over the start and end logits to normalise correctly
mcq.rationale: With hard, non-overlapping splits an answer that happens to straddle a boundary is truncated in every window and can never be recovered. Overlapping by `doc_stride` guarantees the whole span lands inside at least one window, where the start and end heads can select it.
misconceptions: Confuses a correctness safeguard with a throughput optimisation
CORRECT
Invents a deduplication role; overlapping windows deliberately repeat text rather than remove it
Misattributes span-boundary coverage to softmax normalisation

mcq.stem: Your NMT decoder uses beam search that ranks completed hypotheses by the sum of their token log-probabilities. For long source sentences the chosen translations are systematically too short, dropping trailing content. What is the underlying cause and the standard remedy?
options: A brevity penalty baked into the training loss biases the model short; retrain without that term
A too-wide beam surfaces rare long hypotheses; reduce `num_beams` to correct the output length
The tokenizer under-segments long inputs; switch to smaller subword units to lengthen output
Each extra token adds another log-probability below 0, so summed scores favour shorter hypotheses; apply length normalisation (a length penalty on the beam score)
mcq.rationale: Every generated token contributes a log-probability at most 0, so extending a hypothesis can only lower its total score; beam search therefore prefers shorter completions and emits `<eos>` early. Normalising the score by sequence length â€” a length penalty â€” removes the systematic bias so longer translations compete on equal footing.
misconceptions: Invents a brevity penalty inside the MT training loss; BLEU's brevity penalty is an eval-time metric, not a training term
Blames beam width; a wider beam exposes the short-hypothesis bias but is not its root cause
Misattributes a decoding-score bias to subword segmentation granularity
CORRECT

mcq.stem: You are building a keyword search index over Arabic customer reviews. Recall is poor because the same word is written with different Alef and Ya forms, e.g. `Ø£Ø­Ù…Ø¯`/`Ø§Ø­Ù…Ø¯` and `Ù…ØµØ·ÙÙ‰`/`Ù…ØµØ·ÙÙŠ`. Which preprocessing step most directly fixes the mismatch described?
options: Apply orthographic normalisation, unifying Alef variants (`Ø£Ø¥Ø¢`â†’`Ø§`), final `Ù‰`â†’`ÙŠ` and `Ø©`â†’`Ù‡`, before indexing
Restore diacritics (`tashkeel`) on every token so the surface forms line up
Stem each word down to its triliteral root before indexing
Convert the text to Arabic Presentation Forms-B so the glyphs become canonical
mcq.rationale: Alef-hamza spellings (`Ø£ Ø¥ Ø¢`) and final `Ù‰` vs `ÙŠ` (and `Ø©` vs `Ù‡`) are orthographic variants of one word. Folding them to a canonical form before indexing collapses the variants so query and document tokens match, raising recall.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Believes diacritisation unifies spellings, when it adds variation and the reviews are already undiacritized
Confuses light orthographic normalisation with heavier morphological root reduction, which over-conflates distinct words
Reverses Unicode normalisation: presentation forms are positional glyphs to fold away (via NFKC), not a canonical target

mcq.stem: A multilingual RAG service uses a SentencePiece subword tokenizer trained mostly on English text. For the same information content, documents in a low-resource, non-Latin script consume 3-4x more tokens than English, inflating cost and exhausting the context window. What is the primary cause?
options: The language is inherently more information-dense, so more tokens are genuinely required
UTF-8 stores non-Latin scripts in more bytes, and a model's token count equals its byte count
The model pads non-Latin sequences to a fixed per-script block length
The tokenizer's vocabulary under-represents that script, so its words fragment into many short subwords (high fertility), sometimes down to byte-fallback tokens
mcq.rationale: A subword vocabulary learned mostly from English lacks merges for the other script, so its words split into many short pieces, often single characters or byte-fallback tokens. Fertility (tokens per word) rises, inflating sequence length, cost and context use for identical content.
misconceptions: Attributes a tokeniser artifact to the language's inherent information density, though the content is identical
Conflates token count with raw UTF-8 byte length; the tokeniser merges bytes into subwords, so the two differ
Invents fixed per-script padding, whereas transformer sequences are variable-length up to the context limit
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Most Arabic text on the web (news, social posts) is written without short-vowel diacritics (`harakat`). What is the main consequence of this convention for an Arabic NLP pipeline?
options: The text cannot be tokenised until the diacritics are algorithmically restored
One undiacritized surface form can correspond to several readings or meanings, so homograph ambiguity rises
The text becomes invalid UTF-8 because the vowel code points are missing
Each word automatically reduces to its three-letter root
mcq.rationale: Short vowels disambiguate an otherwise identical consonant skeleton, so dropping them lets one form such as `ÙƒØªØ¨` map to several readings (`kataba`, `kutiba`, `kutub`). Tokenisation and encoding still work; the problem is lexical and semantic ambiguity.
misconceptions: Overstates the dependency: tokenisation runs fine on undiacritized text, and diacritisation is a separate optional step
CORRECT
Confuses optional combining harakat with UTF-8 validity, though undiacritized text is well-formed Unicode
Confuses missing diacritics with morphological root extraction (stemming)

mcq.stem: You need semantic search where an English query retrieves relevant documents written in Arabic and French, without running machine translation at query time. Which approach is designed to make this work?
options: Embed everything with a strong monolingual English model and rely on shared loanwords across the corpora
Build a separate BM25 index per language and union the top results
Embed queries and documents with a multilingual sentence-embedding model (e.g. LaBSE, multilingual-E5) that places cross-lingual paraphrases near each other in one shared vector space
Train one monolingual embedding model per language and average their output vectors into a shared index
mcq.rationale: Multilingual sentence encoders are trained so that translations and paraphrases across languages land close together in a single shared vector space, so an English query vector sits near its Arabic and French equivalents, enabling retrieval without translating at query time.
misconceptions: Assumes a monolingual space transfers across languages via loanwords, but vectors for translations will not align
Relies on lexical overlap that does not exist between an English query and an Arabic document
CORRECT
Thinks independently trained spaces share axes; their coordinate systems are incompatible, so averaging is meaningless

mcq.stem: You are evaluating a BIO-tagged named-entity recognition model, and plain token-level accuracy looks excellent. Why is entity-level F1, as computed by `seqeval`, the more informative metric here?
options: Entity-level F1 awards partial credit whenever a predicted span merely overlaps a gold entity, giving a fairer score than exact token matching.
Token accuracy is undefined when the model emits a label sequence of a different length from the gold annotation.
Token accuracy is dominated by the majority `O` tag, so a model that rarely predicts an entity still scores high; entity-level F1 credits only spans whose boundaries and type match exactly.
Entity-level F1 is easier to compute because it collapses the `B-`/`I-` prefixes and scores each tag independently of its span.
mcq.rationale: Most tokens in a sentence carry the `O` (outside) tag, so a model that predicts `O` almost everywhere already matches the gold labels on the large majority of tokens and posts a high token accuracy that says little about extraction. `seqeval`'s entity-level F1 counts a true positive only when a predicted span's boundaries and type match a gold entity exactly, so it reflects how many real entities the model actually recovers.
misconceptions: Believes entity-level scoring gives partial credit for boundary overlap; `seqeval`'s default counts a true positive only on an exact span-and-type match.
Invents a length constraint â€” a tagger emits one label per input token, so predicted and gold sequences are always aligned.
CORRECT
Thinks entity-level F1 discards the BIO structure and scores tags independently, when it requires the whole `B-`/`I-` span to match.

mcq.stem: Your NLI classifier scores 90% on the MNLI dev set but collapses to near-0% on the non-entailment cases of the HANS diagnostic set. What does this most directly indicate?
options: The model has learned a lexical-overlap heuristic â€” predicting `entailment` whenever the hypothesis words all appear in the premise â€” which HANS is built to expose.
The HANS non-entailment examples must be mislabeled, since a model with 90% MNLI accuracy cannot legitimately score near 0%.
The model is overfitting with high variance; training for more epochs on MNLI will close the gap.
HANS uses a different label inventory, so near-0% reflects a label-mapping bug rather than a robustness failure.
mcq.rationale: HANS constructs its non-entailment half specifically so that surface heuristics give the wrong answer. A model that predicts `entailment` whenever the hypothesis tokens all appear in the premise scores well on MNLI yet gets almost every HANS non-entailment case wrong â€” the signature of a learned lexical-overlap shortcut, not mislabeled data or an optimization issue that more epochs would fix.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes high in-distribution accuracy implies clean labels; HANS is deliberately built so heuristic models fail, and is correctly labeled.
Diagnoses a systematic shortcut as ordinary variance overfitting, curable by more epochs on the same biased distribution.
Attributes a heuristic failure to a label-mapping bug, which would depress both entailment and non-entailment, not non-entailment alone.

mcq.stem: You train a binary sentiment classifier on a dataset that is 92% positive, and it reports 92% test accuracy. Before reporting success, what is the single most important thing to check?
options: Whether the learning rate was too high, since a 92% accuracy plateau usually signals an optimization stall.
Whether the test set is large enough for 92% to be statistically significant at `p<0.05`.
Whether the token embeddings were left frozen, since frozen embeddings cap accuracy near the majority-class rate.
Whether the model is merely predicting the majority label â€” on a 92%-positive split an always-`positive` classifier already scores 92%, so inspect per-class precision/recall or macro-F1.
mcq.rationale: On a 92%-positive split the constant classifier that always predicts `positive` already achieves 92% accuracy, so the headline figure can be reached with zero ability to recognize the negative class. Per-class precision/recall or macro-F1 reveals whether the minority class is ever detected.
misconceptions: Reads a majority-class artifact as an optimization symptom; the ceiling is set by the class prior, not the learning rate.
Reaches for significance testing when the problem is the majority-class baseline, not sampling noise.
Invents a causal link between frozen embeddings and an accuracy ceiling that is actually fixed by the label distribution.
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Your toxicity classifier labels the neutral sentence `I am a gay man` as toxic. Error analysis shows identity terms such as `gay` and `muslim` co-occur mostly with toxic comments in the training set. Which intervention most directly addresses the root cause?
options: Raise the decision threshold so that fewer sentences cross into the toxic class overall.
Add non-toxic training examples that contain these identity terms, breaking the term-to-toxicity correlation the model picked up.
Strip identity terms from every input before classification so they cannot influence the prediction.
Switch the training objective to focal loss so the model concentrates on the hardest examples.
mcq.rationale: The classifier learned to associate identity tokens with the toxic label because the training data seldom shows those tokens in neutral contexts. Injecting neutral examples that contain the same terms breaks that co-occurrence at its source â€” the documented mitigation for unintended bias â€” whereas thresholds, token stripping, and loss reweighting leave the learned association in place.
misconceptions: Treats a targeted spurious association as a global threshold problem; moving the threshold shifts all predictions, not the biased correlation.
CORRECT
Hides rather than fixes the bias â€” removing the terms discards signal and still fails on genuinely toxic uses of them.
Assumes emphasizing hard examples corrects a data-distribution bias, when focal loss can reinforce the majority correlation instead.

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A chat model advertises a 128k-token context window. Your request sends a 120k-token document and sets `max_tokens=16000` for the reply, but the API rejects it before generating anything. What explains the rejection?
options: The context window is one budget shared by the prompt and the completion, so a 120k-token prompt leaves roughly 8k for output and a 16k reply overflows it
`max_tokens` is hard-capped at 4096 on every model, so 16000 is always invalid
The 128k figure counts characters, not tokens, and a 120k-token document already exceeds 128k characters
Input and output are metered separately, so this must instead be a transient rate-limit response
mcq.rationale: The context window bounds the sum of prompt tokens and generated tokens. With 120k consumed by the prompt, only about 8k remain, so requesting a 16k completion pushes the total past 128k and the request is refused before decoding starts.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Invents a universal 4096-token output cap; the ceiling is model-specific and often far higher
Conflates the token budget with a character count
Believes the prompt and the completion draw on independent budgets

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Serving a decoder-only LLM at long context lengths, you profile GPU memory and find it is dominated not by the model weights but by the per-request KV cache, which caps your batch size. Which architectural choice most directly reduces KV-cache memory per token?
options: Increase the number of attention heads so the cache is spread across more of them
Swap the feed-forward activation from GELU to SwiGLU
Grouped-query attention (GQA), where several query heads share a smaller set of key/value heads
Tie the input embedding matrix to the output projection weights
mcq.rationale: The KV cache stores one key and one value vector per key/value head, per layer, per token. GQA cuts the number of distinct key/value heads by letting query heads share them, shrinking the cache proportionally. Adding heads enlarges it; SwiGLU and weight tying change compute and parameter count, not per-token KV memory.
misconceptions: Believes adding heads shrinks the cache, when each additional key/value head enlarges it
Confuses a feed-forward activation swap with attention-cache memory
CORRECT
Confuses parameter-count savings from weight tying with per-token KV-cache memory

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You call a text-generation API to label support tickets and need the same ticket to receive the same label on every call. Which single change most directly makes the decoding deterministic?
options: Set `top_p` to `1.0`, which disables nucleus sampling
Set `temperature` to `0`, so each step greedily selects the highest-probability token
Raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to settle on one answer
Add a `presence_penalty` so the model stops changing its mind between calls
mcq.rationale: At `temperature=0` the scaled logits make the softmax collapse to an argmax, so the model always emits the single most probable token -- greedy, deterministic decoding. `top_p`, `max_tokens`, and penalties only reshape an otherwise stochastic distribution.
misconceptions: Thinks `top_p=1.0` forces determinism; it merely admits the whole vocabulary while sampling continues
CORRECT
Confuses output length with decode-time determinism
Confuses a repetition-control penalty with determinism

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your semantic-search index stores 1536-dimensional document vectors from `text-embedding-3-small`. Hoping to improve recall, you re-encode only incoming queries with a different 1536-d embedding model and leave the stored vectors untouched. Retrieval quality collapses even though every vector is still 1536-d. Why?
options: Matching 1536-d vectors requires both sides to be L2-normalised first, and the new query model returns unnormalised vectors
Two embedding models of equal dimension must be trained on the same data, or cosine similarity flips sign
The approximate-nearest-neighbour index must be rebuilt whenever the query encoder changes, though the stored vectors stay valid
Queries and documents are now produced by different models, so they occupy different vector spaces and their cosine similarities no longer track semantic relatedness
mcq.rationale: Vector search assumes queries and documents are mapped by one model into a single shared space. A different query encoder -- even at the same dimensionality -- places queries in an incompatible geometry, so nearest-neighbour distances stop reflecting meaning. The fix is to re-embed the whole corpus with the new model.
misconceptions: Thinks a magnitude-normalisation mismatch is the cause; cosine similarity already divides out vector magnitude
Invents a shared-training-data requirement and a sign inversion that do not occur
Blames the ANN index structure rather than the incompatible embedding spaces
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A creative-writing endpoint alternates between bland output and incoherent tangents, and you are asked to move it from fixed `top_k` to nucleus sampling. How does `top_p` decide its candidate set differently from `top_k`?
options: It keeps the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability first reaches `p`, so the candidate count grows or shrinks with how peaked the distribution is
It keeps a fixed fraction `p` of the vocabulary by count, e.g. `p=0.1` retains the top 10% of all tokens
It keeps every token whose individual probability exceeds `p`
It rescales the logits so the top token's probability equals `p` before sampling
mcq.rationale: Nucleus sampling ranks tokens by probability and takes the shortest prefix whose probabilities sum to at least `p`. When the model is confident that prefix is short; when it is uncertain it lengthens -- an adaptive count, unlike `top_k`'s fixed one. The distractors describe a fixed vocabulary fraction, a per-token probability floor, and a logit rescale.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses cumulative-probability mass with a fixed count-based fraction of the vocabulary
Confuses the cumulative-mass cutoff with a per-token probability threshold (as in min-p sampling)
Confuses candidate-set selection with temperature-style logit rescaling

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You are capacity-planning a standard dense decoder-only transformer and need to state how two costs grow with prompt length n: the compute for self-attention over the prompt, and the memory held by the KV cache. Which pairing is correct?
options: Both self-attention compute and KV-cache memory grow as O(nÂ²) in the sequence length
Self-attention compute grows as O(nÂ²) while the KV cache grows only as O(n)
Self-attention compute grows as O(n) while the KV cache grows as O(nÂ²)
Both grow as O(n log n), because attention is evaluated with an FFT
mcq.rationale: Every token attends to every earlier token, so the attention score computation is quadratic, O(nÂ²), in prompt length. The KV cache instead stores one key and one value vector per token per layer, so it grows linearly, O(n) -- it holds per-token vectors, not the pairwise score matrix.
misconceptions: Conflates the O(nÂ²) score computation with cache memory, which is linear because it stores per-token vectors, not pairwise scores
CORRECT
Inverts the two scalings
Imagines an FFT-based attention that standard transformers do not use

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You load the base checkpoint `Meta-Llama-3-8B` (not the `-Instruct` variant) and send the single prompt `Write a haiku about autumn.` Instead of a haiku it returns a numbered list of other writing prompts. What best explains this behaviour?
options: The base checkpoint was pretrained only for next-token continuation and never instruction-tuned, so it extends the prompt in-distribution â€” here, into more writing prompts â€” instead of obeying it.
The request omits a `system` message; without one, a model defaults to echoing related prompts rather than answering.
Sampling `temperature` is too high, so the model drifts off-task into unrelated text.
An 8B model is too small to compose poetry, so it deflects the instruction into a list.
mcq.rationale: A base checkpoint is optimised only to predict the next token over its pretraining distribution, where a standalone line like `Write a haiku about autumn.` most often sits inside lists of writing prompts â€” so that is what it continues. Supervised instruction tuning is what makes a model treat the line as a directive; the `-Instruct` variant (or a few-shot exemplar) fixes it.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Believes a `system` message is what converts a base model into an instruction follower
Attributes an instruction-following gap to sampling temperature
Attributes an alignment gap to parameter count rather than instruction tuning

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You switch an extraction service from an instruction-tuned model to a reasoning model (o-series style) and keep `max_completion_tokens` at `256`. Requests now often return an empty `content` string with `finish_reason` of `length`, yet billed output tokens are far above zero. What is happening?
options: Reasoning models return the answer inside the reasoning trace, so an empty `content` is expected â€” you should read the trace instead.
Empty `content` with nonzero billing means a safety filter stripped the answer after generation.
`max_completion_tokens` caps the prompt rather than the output, so `256` truncated your input and dropped the instructions.
The model's internal reasoning tokens count against `max_completion_tokens`, so the hidden reasoning exhausts the 256-token budget before any visible answer is emitted.
mcq.rationale: Reasoning models emit many internal reasoning tokens before the final answer, and those are billed as output and counted against `max_completion_tokens`. A cap of `256` can be spent entirely on reasoning, so generation stops with `finish_reason: length` and empty `content`. Raising the cap to leave headroom for reasoning plus the answer resolves it.
misconceptions: Thinks the user-visible answer lives in the reasoning trace rather than `content`
Misreads a length-based truncation as a moderation block
Confuses the output-token cap with an input/context-length limit
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A chat model configured with a `get_weather` tool responds to `What's the weather in Cairo?` with an assistant message whose `tool_calls` holds `get_weather({"city": "Cairo"})`. At this point in an OpenAI-style function-calling flow, what has the model actually done?
options: It executed `get_weather` on the provider's servers, and the `tool_calls` payload carries the returned weather data.
It emitted a request â€” the tool name and JSON arguments â€” that your application must execute, feeding the result back in a `tool` message before the model can answer.
It produced the final user-facing answer; `tool_calls` is metadata recording which tool was used.
It registered the tool for the session, so later turns invoke it automatically without further messages.
mcq.rationale: Function calling is a handshake: the model only decides that a tool should run and emits its name and JSON arguments. Your code executes the function, appends a `tool` message with the result, and calls the model again so it can compose the final answer. The provider never runs your function.
misconceptions: Believes the provider executes the tool server-side and returns its output
CORRECT
Thinks `tool_calls` annotates an already-final answer rather than pausing for execution
Confuses emitting a tool call with registering a tool for automatic invocation

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A document-QA service sends full-resolution page screenshots to a vision-language model with the image `detail` set to `high`, and input-token cost climbs sharply with page size. Why does image resolution drive token cost in these models?
options: Higher-resolution images take longer to transfer, and the API bills the extra transfer time as tokens.
The model runs OCR whose character count grows with resolution, and each recognised character becomes a token.
At `detail: high` the image is split into fixed-size tiles, each encoded as a block of visual tokens, so more pixels yield more tiles and more input tokens.
Larger images inflate the output-token count, because the model must describe more visual content.
mcq.rationale: A vision-language model encodes an image as visual tokens. At `detail: high` the image is partitioned into fixed-size tiles, each turned into a fixed block of tokens, so token count â€” and input cost â€” grows with the number of tiles the resolution produces. `detail: low` downsamples to one small, fixed-cost representation regardless of the original size.
misconceptions: Conflates network transfer time with token accounting
Assumes image cost equals per-character OCR tokens
CORRECT
Attributes input-image token cost to the output side

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: In your agent loop the model returns one assistant message whose `tool_calls` array holds two entries (a parallel tool call). You execute both functions but append only a single `tool` message â€” for the first `tool_call_id` â€” and immediately request the next completion. The API rejects it with a `400`. What is the fix?
options: Merge both function outputs into a single `tool` message carrying a JSON array of the two results.
Set `parallel_tool_calls: false`; the model may not emit more than one call in a message, which caused the rejection.
Return the results in a `user` message, since `tool` messages are only valid immediately after the `system` prompt.
Append one `tool` message per `tool_call_id` â€” both results â€” before requesting the next completion.
mcq.rationale: When an assistant message carries multiple `tool_calls`, the API requires a matching `tool` message for each `tool_call_id` before the conversation may continue; leaving one unanswered makes the transcript invalid, hence the `400`. Supplying both results â€” one message per call id â€” restores a valid sequence, and the model then integrates them.
misconceptions: Thinks parallel results are batched into one message rather than one per `tool_call_id`
Believes the rejection is about parallel calls being unsupported rather than an unanswered call
Uses the wrong role and ordering for returning tool results
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Porting a task to a reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1 / o-series style), your team keeps its tuned prompt of eight worked few-shot examples, each showing a full step-by-step reasoning trace. Zero-shot accuracy on the same model is measurably higher. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: Reasoning models already generate their own extended chain-of-thought; injected few-shot reasoning traces conflict with that learned policy and are documented to lower accuracy versus direct zero-shot instructions.
Eight worked examples overflow the context window, truncating the actual question so the model answers a partial prompt.
Few-shot examples raise the effective sampling `temperature`, making outputs more random and less accurate.
The model overfits the eight examples it was shown and simply repeats their answers.
mcq.rationale: Reasoning models are trained, typically with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes, to produce their own long chain-of-thought. Hand-written few-shot reasoning traces push against that learned policy; the DeepSeek-R1 report and OpenAI's o-series guidance both document that few-shot CoT prompting tends to reduce reasoning-model accuracy, and recommend concise zero-shot instructions.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Attributes the drop to context-window overflow from a handful of examples
Believes few-shot exemplars change the sampling temperature
Conflates in-context examples with training-time memorisation/overfitting

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your team wants to self-host and fine-tune a Llama-family model inside a commercial product. A teammate argues that because the weights are freely downloadable, the model is 'open source' with no usage terms to worry about. Which statement most accurately corrects this?
options: Freely downloadable weights are effectively public domain, so no license terms constrain commercial use

The weights ship under a custom community license with an acceptable-use policy and conditions (such as a monthly-active-user threshold that triggers a separate Meta license), making it 'open-weight', not OSI-approved open source
Because the training code is not released, the license automatically defaults to standard `MIT` terms
'Open source' and 'open weight' are interchangeable labels; both guarantee unrestricted commercial reuse
mcq.rationale: Downloadable weights are not the same as OSI open source. Llama-family weights are released under a custom community license that carries an acceptable-use policy and conditions such as a monthly-active-user threshold requiring a separate Meta license. 'Open weight' describes availability of the parameters, not unrestricted rights, so self-hosting and fine-tuning still incur obligations.
misconceptions: Assumes a downloadable artifact carries no license, ignoring the terms distributed alongside the weights
CORRECT
Invents an `MIT` default; the absence of training code does not change the license actually attached to the weights
