Conflates open-weight availability with the redistribution and reuse guarantees of an OSI-approved license

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You prototype with Ollama on a laptop, one request at a time, and latency is fine. Moving to production you must serve many concurrent users cost-effectively on a single GPU. Which change most directly improves aggregate throughput?
options: Raise `max_tokens` so each request completes in fewer forward passes
Increase sampling `temperature` to speed up token selection
Launch one Ollama process per request on the same GPU so they run in parallel
Serve with an engine that does continuous batching and paged KV-cache management (e.g. vLLM or TGI), so concurrent requests share GPU compute
mcq.rationale: Aggregate throughput on one GPU comes from serving many requests together. Continuous batching interleaves requests at the token level and a paged KV cache (PagedAttention) packs their attention state efficiently, keeping the GPU saturated. Replicating the process reloads the whole model and contends for the same memory and compute, while sampling and length parameters change per-request work, not concurrency.
misconceptions: Confuses per-request length with aggregate throughput; a larger `max_tokens` increases total work rather than reducing it
Treats a sampling parameter as a performance lever; `temperature` has no bearing on throughput
Assumes process-level parallelism helps, but each process reloads the full model and they contend for one GPU with no shared batching
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: To call several LLM vendors without rewriting your request code, you keep using the OpenAI Python SDK but point `base_url` at each vendor's endpoint. For this to work, what must the target vendor provide?
options: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint that accepts the same `/v1/chat/completions` request and response schema
A signed agreement with OpenAI to license its client library
The identical model weights that sit behind OpenAI's own endpoint
A DNS record that rewrites your JSON payload into their native format in transit
mcq.rationale: Repointing the OpenAI SDK sends the same request shape to a different server; it only works when that server implements the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` contract. The SDK does not translate protocols, and neither the underlying model nor DNS is involved in matching the wire format.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Imagines a licensing dependency where only wire-format compatibility is required
Confuses API-schema compatibility with the served model being the same one
Attributes payload translation to DNS, which only resolves hostnames and never touches the request body

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You need to run a 7-billion-parameter open-weight model locally on a GPU with 8 GB of VRAM, but loading it in 16-bit precision fails with an out-of-memory error. What is the standard fix, and why does it work?
options: Lower the sampling `temperature`; deterministic decoding uses less weight memory
Reduce `max_tokens`, because weight storage scales with the number of output tokens
Load a 4-bit quantized build (e.g. a GGUF `Q4` file), which cuts weight memory to roughly a quarter of fp16 for a modest quality cost
Move inference to the CPU, which eliminates the model's memory footprint entirely
mcq.rationale: Weight memory is roughly parameter count times bytes per parameter. At fp16 a 7B model needs about 14 GB, over the 8 GB budget; a 4-bit build stores about half a byte per parameter, roughly 3.5 GB, which fits with room left for the KV cache. `temperature` and `max_tokens` do not change the weight footprint, and CPU inference still requires the weights to occupy system RAM.
misconceptions: Confuses a sampling parameter with memory usage; `temperature` has no effect on the weight footprint
Conflates fixed weight memory with the KV cache; the weights do not scale with `max_tokens`
CORRECT
Thinks CPU inference is memory-free, but the weights must still be held in system RAM

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your service routes every LLM call through a unified client (e.g. LiteLLM) that exposes one interface across OpenAI, Anthropic, and a self-hosted vLLM model â€” you build one `messages` array and receive one normalized response object. Which concern does this abstraction NOT remove?
options: Normalizing each provider's distinct response envelope into that common object

Behavioral parity â€” identical prompts and parameters can still yield materially different quality, output formatting, and tool-calling reliability across models, so prompts and parsing often need per-model tuning
Translating your `messages` array into each vendor's native request body
Applying each provider's authentication scheme on the outbound request
mcq.rationale: A provider-abstraction layer normalizes the transport: request serialization, credentials, streaming, and the response envelope. It cannot make different models behave identically â€” quality, formatting, and tool-calling reliability vary by model, so the prompt and any downstream parsing still need per-model attention.
misconceptions: Names a transport task the abstraction explicitly handles â€” response-envelope normalization
CORRECT
Names request serialization, which the unified client performs for each vendor
Names credential handling, which the client manages per provider via configured keys

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You plan to prompt a strong model at scale to generate a synthetic instruction-tuning dataset, then train a separate in-house model on that data and ship it commercially. Before choosing between a hosted frontier API and a downloadable open-weight model, which constraint most directly governs whether this plan is permissible?
options: Whether the chosen model exposes a context window large enough to hold the full synthetic dataset in one request
Whether generation was run at `temperature` above 0, since only stochastic outputs can be owned by the caller
Nothing â€” model outputs are uncopyrightable, so no provider terms or model license can restrict how you reuse them

Whether the provider's terms of service or the model's license permit using generated outputs to train or improve a competing model, since many hosted terms and several open-weight licenses restrict such 'distillation'
mcq.rationale: Whether you may reuse a model's outputs to train another model is governed by contract, not by the model's runtime capabilities. Hosted providers' terms of service and several open-weight licenses restrict using outputs to build competing models ('distillation'), so the plan's permissibility turns on reading those specific terms â€” independent of context size, sampling settings, or the copyrightability of the generated text.
misconceptions: Confuses a runtime capacity limit with a licensing question; context size does not govern permitted reuse of outputs
Invents a temperature-ownership rule; sampling settings do not determine usage rights
Overgeneralizes from copyrightability to contract; terms of service and license clauses can still bind reuse regardless
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You must pick an LLM to extract structured fields from scanned insurance claims. You rank three candidates by their published MMLU and Chatbot Arena Elo scores, deploy the top-ranked one, and find its field-level extraction accuracy in production is disappointing. What is the primary methodological flaw in how you selected the model?
options: The Elo and MMLU scores should have been combined into a single weighted composite before ranking, rather than compared separately
The public benchmarks were run at a higher temperature than your production setting, so re-running them at `temperature=0` would reorder the candidates correctly
Generic leaderboard scores don't predict performance on your specific task and data distribution; selection should be driven by a held-out eval set of your own labelled claims
MMLU is saturated near the ceiling for frontier models, so you should have ranked the candidates by parameter count instead
mcq.rationale: Aggregate benchmarks like MMLU and Arena Elo measure broad knowledge or human preference, not field extraction on your document distribution, and can be inflated by training-data contamination. The only reliable selection signal is a held-out eval set built from your own labelled claims.
misconceptions: Thinks the remedy is aggregating benchmark numbers into a composite rather than questioning benchmark relevance to the task
Attributes the benchmark-to-production gap to a sampling-parameter mismatch rather than task/distribution mismatch
CORRECT
Believes larger parameter count reliably predicts better task-specific accuracy

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You place Provider B behind Provider A as a fallback, triggering B whenever a call to A raises any exception. A batch of requests carries a malformed `tool_choice` field, so A returns `400 Bad Request`; these requests now also hit B, doubling their latency before failing anyway. How should the fallback be scoped?
options: Fall back only on errors signalling provider unavailability -- timeouts, connection errors, `429`, and `5xx`; let deterministic client errors like `400` fail fast without a fallback attempt
Fall back on every error but cap the total attempts at two, so the extra latency stays bounded
Fix the client-side validation so no `400`s are produced, then keep falling back on all exceptions
Route the `400`s to B first, since A validates request schemas more strictly than B
mcq.rationale: A `400` means the request itself is invalid, so it fails identically on any provider; retrying it against B only adds latency and cost. Fallbacks should fire on signals of provider-side failure -- timeouts, connection errors, `429`, and `5xx` -- not on deterministic client errors.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Frames a non-retryable error as an attempt-count problem; still retries a request that cannot succeed on any provider
Fixes one source of `400`s but leaves the fallback firing on every future non-retryable error
Assumes providers differ in accepting a spec-invalid request; a malformed request is rejected everywhere

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Users say your chatbot 'feels sluggish,' even though end-to-end generation time is acceptable. Without switching models, which change most directly improves the latency users actually perceive?
options: Lower the sampling `temperature` so the model commits to each token faster
Increase `max_tokens` so the full answer arrives in a single response
Enlarge the context window so the model needs fewer follow-up turns
Stream the response so the user sees the first tokens immediately, lowering time-to-first-token
mcq.rationale: Perceived latency is dominated by time-to-first-token. Streaming shows tokens as they are generated, so the user starts reading almost immediately even though total generation time is unchanged; `temperature`, `max_tokens`, and context size don't lower -- and a larger `max_tokens` can raise -- time-to-first-token.
misconceptions: Believes sampling `temperature` changes generation speed
Conflates a larger output-token budget with faster delivery; it raises total time rather than lowering latency
Conflates context-window capacity with responsiveness
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: To cut cost you add a router: a lightweight classifier sends each query either to a small cheap model or to a large expensive one. Most traffic is simple FAQ-style questions, with a hard minority mixed in. Which routing policy captures the most cost savings while protecting quality on the hard queries?
options: Send everything to the large model but cache responses, since caching is simpler to run than a router
Default to the small model and escalate to the large model only when the classifier flags the query as hard or the small model's answer fails a confidence/verification check
Split traffic 50/50 between the two models to balance the load evenly
Route by input length, sending long prompts to the small model and short prompts to the large one
mcq.rationale: Because the simple majority dominates traffic, defaulting to the cheap model and escalating only the hard minority -- via a difficulty classifier or a confidence/verification gate -- captures most of the cost saving while routing the queries that need it to the strong model. Even splits and length rules ignore difficulty, and caching only helps repeated queries.
misconceptions: Substitutes caching for difficulty routing; caching helps only repeated queries, not novel simple ones
CORRECT
Treats difficulty-based dispatch as a load-balancing problem
Uses prompt length as a proxy for difficulty and inverts it, sending heavy inputs to the weak model

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Every request to your assistant includes the same 20K-token policy manual plus a short user question, and input cost dominates the bill. You enable your provider's prompt caching but see almost no cache hits. You currently build the prompt as: a line with the current timestamp and request id, then the manual, then the question. Why are you missing the cache, and what fixes it?
options: Prompt caching only discounts output tokens, so a static manual can never be cached; lower `max_tokens` instead
The 20K manual exceeds the cacheable size limit; split it into smaller chunks that are cached separately
Caching is scoped to a single conversation, so independent single-turn requests can never hit it
The changing timestamp and request id sit at the front, so the cacheable prefix differs on every call; move that variable data after the manual (or remove it) so the manual is a stable prefix
mcq.rationale: Prompt caching matches on an exact prefix, so any per-call value at the front -- here a timestamp and request id -- changes the prefix and busts the cache every time. Making the large, unchanging manual the leading prefix (variable data appended after) restores hits, cutting input cost and time-to-first-token; caching discounts the repeated input, not output, and works across independent requests.
misconceptions: Believes prompt caching discounts output tokens rather than the repeated input prefix
Invents a maximum cacheable size; large stable prefixes are precisely what caching targets
Thinks the cache is scoped to one conversation, missing that it is keyed by prefix content across requests
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You compare two models on your 50-item eval set: Model A scores 82%, Model B scores 78%. You conclude A is better and ship it. A teammate objects. What is the strongest methodological objection?
options: A 4-point gap on 50 items is within sampling noise; you need a larger eval and a significance test (e.g. a paired test with confidence intervals) before claiming A is better
Accuracy is the wrong metric here; you should have compared the models by perplexity, which is continuous and more sensitive
You must run each model at least three times and average, because LLM outputs are nondeterministic even at `temperature=0`
The comparison is invalid unless A and B were each scored on a different randomly drawn set of items to avoid cross-contamination
mcq.rationale: With only 50 items a 4-point gap is two examples -- easily explained by sampling variability. A sound comparison uses a larger test set and reports uncertainty, e.g. confidence intervals and a paired significance test on the same items, rather than ranking on raw point estimates. Perplexity doesn't measure task correctness, run-averaging targets a different variance source, and disjoint test sets would throw away the paired comparison.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Proposes perplexity, an intrinsic metric that doesn't measure task correctness and isn't comparable across tokenizers
Recasts a sample-size/statistical-power problem as run-to-run nondeterminism; averaging repeats of the same 50 items doesn't enlarge the test set
Believes the models need disjoint test sets, which discards the paired comparison and adds variance

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your extraction service ends its instructions with `Do not add any explanation or preamble`, yet the model still occasionally emits `Here is the JSON:` before the object. Which change most reliably suppresses the preamble?
options: Repeat `no preamble` three times and put it in ALL CAPS for emphasis
Set `temperature` to `0` so the model stops generating the extra text
Positively specify the contract -- `Respond with only the JSON object, beginning with the character {` -- and prefill the assistant turn with `{`
Move the instruction from the `user` message into the `system` message
mcq.rationale: A prohibition leaves the wanted output underspecified, so the model can satisfy `no preamble` only inconsistently. Stating exactly what the opening tokens must be, and prefilling the assistant turn with `{` so generation begins inside the object, removes the position where a preamble would appear. Emphasis and `temperature` do not constrain the leading tokens.
misconceptions: Believes repetition and capitalisation change adherence more than the specificity of the instruction does
Confuses sampling determinism with instruction adherence -- greedy decoding can still lock in the preamble
CORRECT
Attributes the failure to the message channel rather than the negative phrasing of the instruction

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You assemble a 6-shot sentiment classifier from the 6 highest-confidence labelled rows you had on hand; they happen to be 5 `positive` and 1 `negative`. In production the model over-predicts `positive` on genuinely ambiguous inputs. What is the primary cause?
options: Majority-label bias -- the skewed label frequency in the demonstrations shifts the model's prior toward `positive` independent of the input
The model has memorised the six rows and returns their stored labels for nearby inputs
Six demonstrations is below the threshold at which in-context learning activates
High-confidence rows are too easy, so they carry no usable signal about the `negative` class
mcq.rationale: LLMs are sensitive to the label distribution of in-context examples: an imbalanced demonstration set biases the output distribution toward the majority label regardless of the query. Balancing the label counts across the shots (and, if needed, calibrating) corrects the skew; the number of shots and their difficulty are not the driver here.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses in-context conditioning with weight-level memorisation or retrieval
Invents a minimum-shot threshold below which in-context learning fails to engage
Misattributes the skew to example difficulty rather than to label frequency

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your zero-shot prompt asks the model to convert free-text dates to `YYYY-MM-DD`, but it returns a mix of `03/04/2026`, `Mar 4`, and ISO strings. Without fine-tuning or post-processing code, the most effective first step is to:
options: Increase `max_tokens` so the model has room to format the date correctly
Add a few input->output examples that each show the exact `YYYY-MM-DD` target (few-shot prompting)
Raise `temperature` so the output settles into a consistent format
Send the request twice and keep whichever answer came back first
mcq.rationale: Few-shot demonstrations show the model the exact target format, letting it pattern-match the transformation with no training. Token budget does not affect formatting, and raising `temperature` increases variability rather than reducing it.
misconceptions: Confuses the output-length budget with output formatting
CORRECT
Believes higher `temperature` increases consistency, when it increases randomness
Treats resampling as a formatting fix rather than a source of more variance

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You build a LangChain `PromptTemplate` whose text embeds a literal JSON example, `{"name": "Ada"}`, to demonstrate the desired shape. Rendering fails because the engine tries to treat part of that JSON as a template variable. What is the correct fix?
options: Wrap the whole prompt in a fenced code block so the engine ignores the braces
Describe the JSON shape in prose instead; `PromptTemplate` cannot contain curly braces
Set `temperature=0` so the model stops substituting the variable
Escape the literal braces by doubling them -- write `{{` and `}}` -- so they render as literal characters
mcq.rationale: Format-string-style templates treat `{...}` as substitution fields, so the literal `{"name": ...}` is parsed as a template variable. Doubling the braces (`{{`, `}}`) escapes them to literal `{`/`}`, leaving your declared input variables intact. A code fence is just more text to the parser, and the error has nothing to do with sampling.
misconceptions: Invents a rule that the parser skips braces inside code fences
Believes literal braces are forbidden rather than escapable
Attributes a template-parsing error to model sampling behaviour
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your few-shot prompt is a fixed 3,000-token block of demonstrations followed by a short per-request user query, and you send thousands of such requests to a provider that supports prompt (prefix) caching. To cut input cost and time-to-first-token, you should structure the prompt so that:
options: the per-request query comes first, so the model reads the actual task before the examples
the demonstration order is reshuffled each request to counter position bias
the fixed demonstration block stays at the very start, with only the variable query appended at the end
the demonstrations move into the `system` message while each query goes out as a separate API call
mcq.rationale: Prefix caching keys on a common leading token sequence: only the longest identical prefix across requests can be reused. Keeping the 3,000-token block first and varying only the tail maximises cache hits, cutting both input cost and time-to-first-token. Putting the query first, or shuffling the examples, changes the prefix on every request and defeats the cache.
misconceptions: Puts the variable content first, which breaks the shared cacheable prefix
Sacrifices the stable prefix for a position-bias concern that caching does not require
CORRECT
Splits into a second call, discarding the shared context instead of caching it

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Even with a label-balanced, well-chosen few-shot set, your model's predicted label probabilities remain skewed -- it favours certain answer tokens and the label that appeared last. You want a principled, training-free correction applied at inference. Which method fits?
options: Contextual calibration -- feed a content-free input such as `N/A` through the same prompt, read the label distribution it yields, then apply the affine correction that maps that neutral input to uniform
Keep adding balanced demonstrations until the competing biases cancel out
Set `temperature` to `0` so the argmax label is always taken
Rename the labels to equal-length synonyms so no token is intrinsically favoured
mcq.rationale: Contextual calibration probes the model with a content-free input to expose its prior over the labels; that non-uniform output reveals the majority-, recency-, and common-token bias. Fitting an affine transform that sends the neutral input to a uniform distribution, then applying it to real predictions, cancels the systematic skew. Adding examples or lowering `temperature` shifts or sharpens outputs but leaves the prior in place.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Assumes more demonstrations average out a bias that is systematic, not sampling noise
Confuses decoding determinism with removing a skewed prior over labels
Targets token length while leaving the model's positional and frequency prior untouched

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You elicit JSON from an instruction-tuned model through prompting alone (no constrained-decoding or tool mode available). The data is correct, but the model keeps wrapping it in a ```json code fence preceded by a sentence of preamble, so `json.loads` fails. Which prompt-side technique most directly removes both the preamble and the fence?
options: Add the fence delimiter to the request's `stop` sequences so generation halts at the code fence
Raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to finish and drop the wrapper
Prefill the start of the assistant turn with `{` so decoding continues from inside the JSON object
Append a "respond concisely" instruction to the system prompt
mcq.rationale: The preamble-and-fence is a learned response habit, not a length or sampling artifact. Prefilling the assistant turn with `{` forces the model to continue from inside the object, so it cannot emit a leading sentence or a ```json fence; you then parse (optionally stopping at the matching brace). A `stop` on the fence would halt at the first fence and discard the payload, and `max_tokens` or a brevity instruction only change length probabilistically.
misconceptions: Assumes a `stop` sequence strips a leading preamble/fence when it only halts generation at the first match, cutting off the payload
Treats a learned preamble-and-fence habit as an output-truncation problem
CORRECT
Believes a natural-language brevity instruction reliably suppresses code-fence wrapping

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A team moves an extraction task from prompt-then-parse to strict schema-constrained decoding. JSON parse failures fall to zero, but accuracy on a `category` enum field drops noticeably versus the old approach. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: The schema emits `category` before any free-text field, so token masking forces the label immediately, denying the intermediate reasoning span the free-form output previously allowed
Constrained decoding lowers the effective sampling temperature, collapsing predictions onto the most frequent class
The grammar mask renormalises probabilities toward whichever enum value sorts first alphabetically
Schema validation silently rewrites any out-of-enum prediction to the enum's first value
mcq.rationale: Structured decoding masks tokens that violate the grammar. When `category` is the first field, the model must commit to an enum value with no scratchpad, losing the reasoning tokens the prompt-then-parse pipeline produced before answering. Masking only zeroes disallowed tokens; it does not change temperature, reorder by spelling, or silently rewrite values. The fix is to order a `reasoning` string field before `category`, or keep chain-of-thought then parse.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Conflates token masking with a change in sampling temperature
Believes the grammar mask reweights among allowed tokens rather than only zeroing disallowed ones
Imagines a validation layer mutates predicted values instead of merely constraining generation

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: In a function-calling agent a valid `get_weather(city)` tool is routinely ignored â€” the model answers weather questions from parametric memory instead of calling it. The schema is well-formed. Following tool-instruction best practice, the highest-leverage fix is to:
options: Rename the function to `get_weather_tool_v2` so it is more salient to the model
Write a description stating what the tool returns and when to use it â€” e.g. for any request about current or real-time weather
Make `city` optional so the model can call the tool with fewer arguments
Add today's date to the system prompt so the model treats its own weather knowledge as stale
mcq.rationale: A model decides whether to invoke a tool primarily from its natural-language description. Stating what the tool returns and when to call it is the direct lever. A verbose or versioned name adds no usage guidance, making a required argument optional invites underspecified calls, and telling the model its knowledge is stale still never instructs it to reach for this tool.
misconceptions: Assumes a longer or versioned identifier substitutes for an explicit usage description
CORRECT
Confuses parameter optionality with tool-selection guidance
Confuses making the model aware its knowledge is stale with telling it when to invoke the tool

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You refactor a brittle single prompt into a three-step chain â€” extract entities, normalise them, then draft an email from the normalised entities. Step 1 occasionally invents an entity, and the final email confidently cites it. Which change best exploits the chain's structure to catch this before the email is sent?
options: Merge the three steps back into one prompt so there is no intermediate output to corrupt
Raise `temperature` on the drafting step so the email hedges its claims
Sample the extraction step several times and majority-vote the entities to suppress the invented one
Insert a validation gate after step 1 that checks each extracted entity against the source before the chain continues
mcq.rationale: Chaining exposes intermediate outputs, which is exactly what lets you inspect and gate them. A validation step after extraction â€” programmatic or a verifier LLM â€” grounds each entity against the source and stops a fabricated one from propagating. Merging removes the inspection point, hedging changes tone not grounding, and self-consistency voting reduces variance but cannot catch an entity the model fabricates systematically.
misconceptions: Discards the intermediate hand-offs that make per-step validation possible
Confuses softening the email's tone with catching an upstream factual error
Confuses variance-reducing self-consistency with verifying an entity against the source
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your extraction schema declares `confidence` as `{"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 1}` and you enable strict schema-constrained decoding. Parsing never fails, yet values like `7.4` still reach production. What is happening, and what is the correct fix?
options: The decoder also ignores `type`; store `confidence` as a string and cast it downstream
Grammar-based decoding enforces structure, `type`, required keys and enums but generally not numeric-range keywords, so `minimum`/`maximum` must be checked in a post-generation validation step
`minimum`/`maximum` activate only when `strict` is set on the range object itself; nest another `strict: true` there
The model emitted the number as a string and JSON parsing rounded it into range
mcq.rationale: Constrained decoding compiles a token grammar from structural and type constraints (object shape, `type`, `enum`, `required`) and masks accordingly, but arbitrary value predicates such as numeric bounds aren't expressible in that grammar, so they aren't enforced during generation. `type` is enforced, so the value is a genuine number â€” just unbounded. You validate the range after parsing and clamp or re-prompt. There is no per-keyword `strict` flag, and parsing does not coerce values into range.
misconceptions: Overgeneralises the range-enforcement gap to claim `type` is also unenforced
CORRECT
Invents a nested flag instead of recognising an unsupported constraint class
Assumes JSON parsing coerces or clamps numeric values

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A map-reduce chain summarises each of 40 retrieved chunks (map), then answers the user from the 40 summaries alone (reduce). Precise questions â€” 'what was the exact penalty-clause figure?' â€” fail even when the figure is present in a source chunk, and improving the map-step summary prompt barely helps. What is the fundamental issue and the right fix?
options: The reduce step overflows its context window at 40 summaries; keep only the top 10 summaries
The summaries introduce noise; raise the reduce step's `temperature` so it interpolates the missing figure
Summarisation is lossy compression, so detail dropped in the map step is unrecoverable at reduce; carry forward chunk pointers or verbatim spans so the reduce step can fetch the exact source
The map and reduce steps use different system prompts; unifying them restores the figure
mcq.rationale: Map-step summarisation is lossy: any detail it omits is gone by the reduce step because the source chunk is no longer in view, so no reduce-side prompt tweak can recover it â€” an information-bottleneck property of the summarise-then-answer topology. The fix is architectural: preserve pointers or verbatim spans (or re-fetch the source chunk) so the reduce step grounds on the exact text. Temperature cannot reconstruct absent facts, the window need not be overflowing, and prompt unification does not restore discarded detail.
misconceptions: Misattributes an information-loss failure to context-window overflow
Believes sampling temperature can reconstruct information absent from the context
CORRECT
Blames prompt inconsistency for loss inherent to summarise-then-answer

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: An agent exposes `search_web(query)` and `search_policy_db(query)`, and for internal-policy questions it keeps choosing `search_web`, returning irrelevant hits. Both tools are currently described only as 'Search for information.' Which change most directly fixes the mis-routing?
options: Rewrite each description to state its domain and when to prefer it â€” e.g. `search_policy_db`: the authoritative source for internal company policy, used for any policy question
Remove `search_web` so only the policy tool remains
Add a `router` tool the model must call first to choose between the two
Lower the sampling temperature so the model stops selecting `search_web`
mcq.rationale: Tool choice is driven by the descriptions; two identical 'Search for information' strings give the model nothing to distinguish. Stating each tool's domain and precedence is the direct lever for correct routing. Deleting `search_web` removes needed capability, a `router` tool adds a hop while still needing the domain knowledge the descriptions should carry, and temperature does not encode routing intent.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Drops needed capability instead of disambiguating the two descriptions
Adds an orchestration hop while leaving the undifferentiated descriptions unchanged
Treats a description-semantics problem as sampling randomness

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You assemble a prompt for a model with an 8,192-token context window: a fixed 1,500-token system prompt, retrieved chunks, and the user question, with `max_tokens=1024` reserved for the answer. Which statement correctly describes the token budget available for retrieved chunks?
options: Prompt tokens and the reserved completion share the 8,192-token window, so chunks may use at most `8192 - 1024 - 1500 - question_tokens`.
Only prompt tokens count against the 8,192-token window, so chunks may use `8192 - 1500 - question_tokens`; the completion is billed against a separate limit.
The window caps generated tokens only, so retrieved chunks are effectively unbounded by it.
`max_tokens` caps the whole request, so the entire prompt including chunks must fit within 1,024 tokens.
mcq.rationale: Every major LLM API meters prompt tokens and generated tokens against the same context window, so you must reserve the completion inside it. Subtracting `max_tokens` and the fixed system prompt and question from 8,192 leaves the budget for retrieved chunks.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Believes input and output are metered against independent budgets rather than one shared window
Thinks the context window measures only generated tokens, leaving the prompt unmetered
Confuses `max_tokens` (an output cap) with a ceiling on total request size

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: In a RAG pipeline you concatenate 20 reranked passages into a long-context prompt. Accuracy is high when the gold passage lands near the start or end of the list but drops sharply when it falls in the middle. Which change most directly targets this 'lost-in-the-middle' behavior?
options: Shuffle the passage order randomly on each request so no position is systematically favored.
Increase `top_k` so more passages are retrieved and the gold passage is more likely to be present.
Reorder so the highest-ranked passages occupy the first and last positions and weaker ones fill the middle.
Raise the sampling `temperature` so the model attends over a broader span of the context.
mcq.rationale: Long-context models recall information most reliably from the beginning and end of the input and least reliably from the middle. Placing the strongest passages at both ends puts the likely answer where recall is highest; retrieving more passages only enlarges the weak middle, shuffling still leaves passages there, and `temperature` governs sampling, not attention over positions.
misconceptions: Assumes positional recall bias can be averaged away by randomization rather than exploited through placement
Treats a positional-recall problem as a retrieval-coverage problem, enlarging the neglected middle
CORRECT
Confuses sampling temperature with how the model attends across context positions

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A multi-turn chatbot appends every user and assistant message to the prompt on each turn. After a long session, calls begin to fail because the accumulated history exceeds the model's context window. Which approach keeps the conversation working within the window?
options: Lower `max_tokens` on each response so older history is discarded automatically.
Summarize or evict the oldest turns each round so the running prompt stays under the token limit.
Raise the sampling `temperature`, which packs the history into fewer tokens.
Stream the response as `text/event-stream` so the context-window limit no longer applies.
mcq.rationale: The context window bounds the total prompt, so an ever-growing history must eventually overflow it. A sliding window or a running summary of older turns keeps the prompt within budget while retaining recent context; `max_tokens`, temperature, and streaming all affect the output, not the size of the accumulated input.
misconceptions: Confuses the output-length cap with the size of the accumulated input history
CORRECT
Imagines temperature shrinks the prompt rather than shaping output sampling
Believes response streaming changes how input tokens count against the window

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You enforce a strict input-token budget before each LLM call by estimating tokens as `len(text) / 4`. Requests containing source code and non-English text still overflow the context window and get rejected. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Change the divisor to `len(text) / 3` to build in a larger safety margin.
Strip whitespace before applying the `/ 4` estimate.
Truncate every request to a fixed maximum character length.
Count tokens with the model's own tokenizer (e.g., `tiktoken` for the target model) instead of a characters-per-token heuristic.
mcq.rationale: The characters-per-token ratio is not constant: code, punctuation, and non-Latin scripts often split into far more tokens than English prose, so any fixed divisor mis-estimates them. Encoding the text with the model's actual tokenizer yields the exact token count the API meters against the window.
misconceptions: Keeps a heuristic and only retunes a constant that still mis-estimates atypical text
Assumes whitespace, not the token-to-character ratio, causes the discrepancy
Trades overflow for silent truncation without ever measuring real tokens
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your agent sends an identical 20,000-token system prompt and tool-definition block on every request, followed by a short, varying user turn, and input-token cost and latency are high. Your provider supports prompt caching. How should you structure requests to benefit from it?
options: Move the static block to the end of the request, after the user turn, so it is cached last.
Randomize the order of the static blocks each call to widen cache coverage.
Lower `max_tokens` so the cached prefix fits alongside the completion.
Keep the large static block as an identical prefix at the very start of every request and vary only what follows it.
mcq.rationale: Prompt caching reuses computation for an exact, contiguous prefix and stops at the first token that differs from an earlier request. A long invariant block placed at the very start maximizes the cache hit and is billed at a reduced input rate; putting variable content first, reordering the blocks, or shrinking the output all prevent the prefix from matching.
misconceptions: Treats prefix caching as if it matched a suffix rather than the leading tokens
Assumes caching matches unordered content instead of an exact token sequence
Confuses the output-length cap with what enables prefix reuse
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: To cut prompt size you route every retrieved passage set through an LLM-based contextual compressor before inserting it into the final prompt. For short-context queries, total token spend rises rather than falls, even though the final prompts are smaller. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Compressing the passages changes the cached prefix, so every request now misses the prompt cache and is billed at the full rate.

The compressor call is itself a billed generation -- it reads the passages as input and emits the compressed text as output; for already-short passages that round-trip costs more than it saves downstream.
Shorter final prompts fall into a higher per-token price tier, so fewer tokens cost more.
Compression raises the final model's `max_tokens`, inflating output-token cost.
mcq.rationale: An LLM compressor consumes input tokens (the passages) and produces output tokens (the compressed version) on its own metered call. When the passages are already small, that extra round-trip outweighs the tokens removed from the downstream prompt, so net spend increases. Compression rewrites the variable retrieved suffix, not the cached instruction prefix, so it does not invalidate the cache; per-token price is not length-tiered; and it does not touch the answer model's output cap.
misconceptions: Assumes the compressor rewrites the cached prefix, when it only touches the variable retrieved suffix
CORRECT
Invents length-based per-token pricing tiers
Conflates input-side compression with the output budget `max_tokens`

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Prompts are hard-coded as string literals in your service, so every wording tweak ships through the full build-and-deploy pipeline and only engineers can make one. Product wants to iterate on prompts and roll a bad one back within seconds. Which change delivers this?
options: Move the prompt strings into a relational table and apply each edit as an in-place `UPDATE` to the same row
Load the prompts from environment variables set per environment and edit those values
Store prompts in a prompt-management registry, resolve them at runtime by name and a `production` label, and roll out or roll back by repointing the label to an immutable version -- no code deploy
Wrap each prompt change in a feature flag in the codebase and toggle it at runtime
mcq.rationale: A prompt registry keeps immutable, numbered versions plus a movable label the app resolves at request time, so publishing or rolling back is a metadata change rather than a deploy, and non-engineers can edit in a UI. In-place `UPDATE`s discard history and block rollback; env vars still need a restart and record no versions; feature flags can only toggle prompt text already shipped in code.
misconceptions: Treats an overwriting `UPDATE` as versioning, leaving no prior version to roll back to or audit
Assumes env-var edits avoid a deploy, but they need a restart and record no version history
CORRECT
Believes a flag can introduce new prompt text, though it only switches between variants already deployed in code

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: In an offline eval you use an LLM as a judge to pick the better of two prompt variants' outputs, presenting both in one judge prompt as `Answer A` and `Answer B`. Whichever output occupies the `A` slot is chosen well above 50% of the time, even after you swap which variant is placed there. How do you obtain a fair verdict?
options: Evaluate every pair in both orders -- `(A,B)` and `(B,A)` -- and count a win only when the two runs agree, or average them, cancelling the judge's position bias
Set the judge's `temperature` to `0`; the ordering effect is randomness and disappears once decoding is deterministic
Ask the judge to rate `Answer A` and `Answer B` each on a 1-10 scale within the same prompt and pick the higher score
Provide the judge a gold reference answer for each input so it stops defaulting to the first option
mcq.rationale: LLM judges systematically prefer a position (commonly the first) independent of content. The bias is deterministic, not random, so `temperature=0` only makes it reproducible. Scoring both answers inside one prompt keeps them co-located and equally biased. Running each pair in both orders and requiring agreement (or averaging) cancels the effect.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Mistakes a systematic positional preference for sampling noise; `temperature=0` makes it reproducible, not absent
Assumes switching from choice to in-prompt scoring removes ordering, but co-located answers stay position-biased
Misdiagnoses position bias as a missing-reference issue, which addresses grounding, not ordering

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You version prompts by committing the template text to `git`. Weeks later the same production prompt returns noticeably different answers, yet the fully rendered prompt string is byte-for-byte identical to before. What is the most likely cause?
options: The `git` blob for the template was corrupted; re-checkout the commit to restore the original bytes
The hosted model was rolled forward under the same alias; because output depends on the model version and decoding parameters as well as the text, a reproducible prompt version must pin those too
Committed prompts silently expire after a fixed interval and must be re-published to stay current
The template variables were substituted in a different order, changing the rendered result
mcq.rationale: Model output is a function of the prompt text, the model version, and the generation parameters. Providers advance a model under a stable alias, so identical text can yield different answers over time. Versioning only the template misses this; a reproducible prompt version records the model id/snapshot and decoding params alongside the text.
misconceptions: Reaches for file corruption, which `git` content-addressed storage would already have surfaced; the bytes are intact
CORRECT
Invents an expiry mechanism; committed text does not time out
Blames substitution order even though the rendered string is stated to be identical

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your prompt regression suite runs 50 examples in CI on every prompt PR at `temperature=0`, asserting the model output exactly equals a stored gold string. The suite fails constantly on trivial wording differences that are actually correct answers. What is the right fix?
options: Increase the gold set to 500 examples so the occasional exact-match miss is a smaller fraction of the score
Set `top_p` to `1.0` so decoding becomes deterministic and the outputs match the gold strings
Regenerate and overwrite the gold outputs at the start of each CI run so they always match

Replace exact-string equality with behavioral assertions -- JSON-schema validity, required-fact presence, or a semantic-similarity/LLM-judge threshold -- so acceptable paraphrases pass while genuine regressions still fail
mcq.rationale: Open-ended LLM output rarely matches a single gold string verbatim, so exact equality flags valid paraphrases as failures. Regression suites (e.g., `promptfoo`) assert properties -- schema validity, required content, or similarity above a threshold -- capturing the requirement without over-fitting to one phrasing.
misconceptions: Assumes brittleness averages out with scale, but every added case is still exact-match and flaky
Believes `top_p=1.0` yields determinism; it disables nucleus truncation and paraphrase variation remains
Overwriting the baseline each run destroys the reference, so no regression can ever be detected
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Comparing two prompts on a 40-example eval set, v2 scores 33/40 and v1 scores 32/40. A teammate wants to ship v2 as the better prompt. What is the sound way to act on this result?
options: Ship v2 -- a higher score on the eval set is by definition evidence of better generalization
Keep v1 -- a fixed rule of thumb says a challenger must beat the incumbent by at least 10 points to justify a change
Treat a 33/40-vs-32/40 gap as within sampling error at n=40; enlarge the eval set or run a paired significance test such as McNemar's before concluding v2 is better
Re-run both prompts at a higher `temperature` and keep whichever wins more runs
mcq.rationale: A one-example difference on 40 items sits well inside the confidence interval and could easily flip on a new sample. A paired test on the shared examples, or a larger eval set, is what distinguishes signal from noise; fixed-margin heuristics and temperature changes do not address the statistical question.
misconceptions: Equates a within-noise eval-set lead with generalization, ignoring the confidence interval at n=40
Substitutes an arbitrary fixed-margin rule for a significance test appropriate to the sample size
CORRECT
Confuses sampling uncertainty with decoding randomness; varying `temperature` doesn't test significance

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your prompt regression suite pins a dated model snapshot, runs `promptfoo` assertions at `temperature=0`, and gates merges in CI. An edit that fixes the one failing case turns the suite green and is merged, but production quality then drops on inputs the suite never contained. What does the green suite actually tell you?
options: That decoding is non-deterministic at `temperature=0`; raise the samples-per-case so flaky passes are caught

Only that no regression occurred on the cases it covers; the suite under-samples the production distribution, so tuning the prompt to its visible cases over-fit them -- the remedy is to grow the eval set from real traffic and keep a holdout, not to treat a pass as proof of no regression
That the pinned snapshot has drifted; move to a newer snapshot and re-baseline the assertions
That the assertions are too strict; loosen the thresholds so the suite reflects real behavior
mcq.rationale: A regression suite certifies only the inputs it contains. Passing means 'no regression on these cases,' not 'no regression.' Editing the prompt to satisfy the visible failures can degrade the unsampled tail -- a Goodhart/over-fitting effect. Keeping the suite representative by sampling cases from production and maintaining a holdout is what lets it track the real input distribution.
misconceptions: Blames non-determinism though the suite passed deterministically; the gap is coverage, not variance
CORRECT
Attributes an unrepresented-input problem to model drift, despite the pinned snapshot and a passing suite
Loosening thresholds hides failures rather than covering the missing inputs

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: To defend a RAG assistant against indirect prompt injection, an engineer wraps every retrieved chunk in `<untrusted>...</untrusted>` tags and adds a system instruction never to obey instructions that appear between those tags. Why is this delimiting technique, on its own, not a dependable security boundary?
options: Custom XML tags are stripped by the tokenizer before inference, so the model never actually sees the boundary markers.
The extra tag tokens inflate the prompt and eventually evict the trusted system instructions once the context window fills.
Instructions and data share one undifferentiated token stream, so a forceful injected directive â€” or one that spoofs the closing `</untrusted>` tag â€” can still override the rule.
Delimiting only works on a fine-tuned model; a base model treats the tags as literal text and ignores the rule entirely.
mcq.rationale: Delimiters help the model tell roles apart and reduce accidental instruction-following, but they are not enforced. An LLM has no privileged channel: the system rule and the injected payload compete as ordinary tokens, so a persuasive or delimiter-spoofing payload can win. Treat delimiting as one layer and gate consequential actions with controls outside the model.
misconceptions: Believes the tokenizer discards markup rather than encoding it as tokens the model attends to
Answers a security-boundary question with an unrelated context-window eviction mechanism
CORRECT
Assumes delimiter-following is a fine-tuning artifact rather than general in-context behaviour

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: An autonomous email agent can read a user's inbox and call a `send_email(to, body)` tool. A malicious message hides text instructing the agent to forward recent one-time passcodes to an external address, and in testing the agent complies. Which mitigation most reliably prevents this class of exfiltration?
options: Enforce a deterministic policy outside the model â€” a recipient allowlist plus human confirmation for any `send_email` to a new address â€” so a compromised model still cannot complete the send.
Add a capitalised, emphatic system rule instructing the agent never to act on instructions found in email bodies.
Route the task to a larger, more capable model that is better at recognising manipulative content.
Set the sampling `temperature` to `0` so the agent behaves deterministically and predictably.
mcq.rationale: Injection cannot be reliably eliminated inside the model, because instructions and untrusted data share one context and nothing guarantees the model disobeys a convincing payload. The durable defence removes the model's unilateral power to cause harm: least-privilege tools, recipient allowlists, and human approval for consequential, irreversible actions. Prompt hardening, a bigger model, and temperature are not security controls.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Treats prompt hardening as a security boundary; a persuasive injection can still override system wording
Assumes injection is a capability gap, but more capable models follow convincing injections too
Confuses sampling determinism with a security guarantee

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A support assistant assembles each prompt from four sources. Which one is untrusted context that could carry an indirect prompt-injection payload?
options: The developer's system prompt that sets the assistant's role and rules.
The body of a third-party web page fetched at query time and pasted into the context.
The hard-coded `JSON` schema the developer requires the response to follow.
The tool definitions the developer registered with the model.
mcq.rationale: Untrusted context is any text originating outside the developer's control that an attacker could author â€” retrieved documents, fetched web pages, tool results, user uploads. A fetched web page can hide instructions that the model then follows (indirect injection). The system prompt, developer-defined schema, and tool definitions are authored by the developer and are trusted.
misconceptions: Treats the developer-authored system prompt as an attack surface rather than trusted content
CORRECT
Confuses a developer-defined output contract with attacker-controllable input
Confuses developer-registered tool definitions with attacker-controllable input

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A code-review agent is asked by a developer to summarise a public pull request. The PR description contains hidden text that makes the agent post an approving comment and merge the PR; the developer who invoked the agent never wrote that text. This incident is best classified as:
options: A jailbreak, because the agent bypassed its built-in safety guardrails.
A direct prompt injection, since the malicious instruction reached the model through its prompt.
A hallucination, since the agent performed an action nobody explicitly requested.
An indirect prompt injection, since attacker instructions entered through untrusted content the agent ingested.
mcq.rationale: Indirect prompt injection is when malicious instructions arrive inside third-party content the model ingests â€” a PR description, web page, email, or document â€” rather than from the operator. Direct injection is when the person interacting with the model types the instruction themselves. Jailbreaking specifically subverts safety training; hallucination is unsupported fabrication. Naming the vector correctly drives the fix: treat that content as untrusted and gate the merge behind approval.
misconceptions: Conflates following attacker instructions in data with jailbreaking, which subverts safety training
Misses that the payload arrived via ingested third-party content, not the operator's own input â€” that is indirect, not direct
Confuses attacker-controlled instruction-following with unsupported fabrication
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You split technical manuals with a fixed-size splitter set to 512 tokens and `chunk_overlap=0`, cutting at exact token boundaries. Users report answers arrive cut mid-explanation: the top-ranked chunk holds the start of a procedure but not its final step. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Lower the chunk size to 128 tokens so each chunk is more focused
Raise `top_k` so more chunks are retrieved and concatenated together
Set a `chunk_overlap` (e.g. 64 tokens) so content spanning a boundary stays intact in the adjacent chunk
Switch to an embedding model with a larger maximum sequence length
mcq.rationale: Zero-overlap fixed splitting can slice one coherent passage across two chunks, so neither chunk alone holds the whole answer. An overlap window duplicates the boundary region into the neighbouring chunk, so at least one retrieved chunk contains the passage intact.
misconceptions: Thinks smaller chunks fix boundary loss, when they only create more boundaries for a passage to be split across
Assumes retrieving more chunks reassembles a split passage, ignoring that the second half may not rank or sit adjacent
CORRECT
Confuses the embedding model's input limit with how the splitter places chunk boundaries

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You ingest born-digital, two-column research papers using a basic PDF extractor that returns glyphs in the order they were drawn on the page. The resulting chunks interleave sentences from the left and right columns, and retrieval is poor. What is the root cause?
options: The extractor emits text in draw order, not reading order, so a two-column layout interleaves the columns; you need a layout-aware parser that reconstructs reading order
The pages are scanned images, so no text exists until you run OCR over them first
The chunk size is too large, so unrelated paragraphs are being merged into one chunk
The embedding model lacks the domain vocabulary, so similar chunks are scored inconsistently
mcq.rationale: A two-column page stores text runs in the order they were placed, not the order a human reads them. A naive extractor concatenates those runs and interleaves the columns. Layout-aware parsing detects the column regions and emits text in reading order before chunking ever happens.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses a reading-order defect in born-digital text with a scanned-image problem that needs OCR
Attributes the interleaving to chunk size, though the text is already scrambled before it is chunked
Blames the embedding model for a defect introduced upstream during text extraction

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your team must answer employee questions from an internal policy handbook that is edited several times a week, and every answer has to cite the exact clause it came from. You are weighing weekly fine-tuning of the base model on the handbook against a RAG pipeline over it. Which property of this task most favours RAG?
options: RAG will consume fewer tokens per request than a fine-tuned model answering the same question
RAG removes the need to evaluate answer quality once the index is built
A fine-tuned model cannot answer factual questions at all, leaving RAG as the only option
The source changes frequently and answers must cite specific clauses, which RAG serves by retrieving the current document at query time
mcq.rationale: RAG fetches the live document at query time, so edits are reflected immediately without retraining and the retrieved passage is right there to cite. Weekly fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights, always lags the latest edits, and leaves nothing concrete to cite.
misconceptions: Believes RAG lowers per-request tokens, when injecting retrieved context typically enlarges the prompt
Assumes a built index removes the need to evaluate answer quality
Overstates fine-tuning's limits: it can encode facts, just not cite them or update cheaply
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You crawl your product's HTML documentation and index a plain HTML-to-text conversion of each page. Retrieval keeps surfacing navigation menus, the cookie banner, and footer links instead of the article body. Which change at ingestion time helps most?
options: Lowercase the extracted text and strip stopwords before embedding it
Extract the main content region (e.g. with `trafilatura` or a readability algorithm) and index only that, dropping the surrounding chrome
Increase `top_k` so the real content is more likely to appear somewhere in the results
Store each page's URL in chunk metadata so results can be filtered afterwards
mcq.rationale: The boilerplate is being embedded as though it were content, so it competes with the article for retrieval. Main-content extraction removes navigation, banners, and footers before indexing, so only the substantive text is ever embedded and returned.
misconceptions: Applies classic bag-of-words cleaning that neither removes boilerplate nor helps dense embeddings
CORRECT
Retrieves more results without removing the boilerplate that is polluting them
Adds metadata that supports filtering but does nothing to stop boilerplate being embedded as content

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Evaluation reveals a tension: embedding small (roughly two-sentence) chunks makes retrieval land on the exact relevant sentence, but the retrieved chunk is then too short for the LLM to produce a complete, grounded answer. You want both precise retrieval and enough surrounding context. Which pattern resolves this directly?
options: Embed and match on the small child chunks, but pass the larger parent chunk (or a surrounding window) to the LLM
Re-embed everything at a single large chunk size so each chunk already carries full context
Increase overlap to roughly 50% so neighbouring small chunks share most of their text
Raise `top_k` and concatenate many small chunks until the context is long enough
mcq.rationale: The retrieval unit and the generation unit need not be the same. Small-to-big (parent-document / sentence-window) retrieval indexes fine-grained child chunks for precise matching, then substitutes the parent chunk or a surrounding window at generation time so the model receives full context.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Restores context by enlarging chunks but discards the retrieval precision that small chunks provided
Bloats the index with near-duplicate chunks yet still returns short, possibly non-contiguous context
Concatenates scattered neighbours that may be irrelevant or non-adjacent, with no guarantee of coherent context

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A business analyst asks your support-ticket assistant: 'Across all 4,000 tickets filed last quarter, what were the three most common root causes?' Your pipeline embeds the query, retrieves the top 8 chunks by cosine similarity, and asks the LLM to summarise them. The answer is confidently wrong every time. Why does this architecture systematically fail this class of question?
options: The embedding model truncates long tickets, so the root-cause text is dropped before indexing
The cosine-similarity cut-off is too strict, filtering relevant tickets out of the top 8
The query needs an aggregate over the whole corpus, but top-k retrieval returns only a small similar sample, so the model never sees the full distribution to count over
Reranking the 8 chunks with a cross-encoder would surface the true root causes
mcq.rationale: This is a global, analytical query: it asks for a count over every ticket. Top-k semantic retrieval is built to fetch a few passages most similar to the query, not to enumerate a corpus, so the model reasons over a biased 8-chunk sample. Such questions need a different design, e.g. structured extraction plus aggregation (text-to-SQL) or a map-reduce pass over all tickets.
misconceptions: Blames per-document embedding truncation for what is a corpus-level retrieval-coverage limitation
Assumes tuning the similarity threshold changes the fact that only a handful of chunks are ever returned
CORRECT
Thinks reranking a tiny sample can recover a statistic that requires scanning the whole corpus

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your RAG service instructs the LLM to append a `[chunk_id]` marker after each sentence, drawn from the ids you injected beside the retrieved passages. In evaluation you find sentences whose `[chunk_id]` points to a passage that does not actually support them. Which check most reliably catches these before the answer ships?
options: Raise the retrieval `top_k` so the model has more passages available to cite
Set `temperature` to 0 so the model attaches citations deterministically
Run an entailment (NLI) check that each cited passage supports its sentence, and drop or flag the citations that fail
Strengthen the instruction to 'cite only passages that support the sentence,' with a few-shot example
mcq.rationale: The defect is a citation whose passage does not support its sentence, which only an independent check can catch: verify that each cited passage entails the sentence it is attached to. Prompt wording, `temperature`, and `top_k` shape generation but never confirm that the emitted citation actually supports the claim.
misconceptions: Confuses retrieval recall with citation faithfulness; more candidate passages do not validate the one the model chose
Mistakes deterministic output for correct output; a fixed citation can still be unsupported
CORRECT
Treats a verification gap as a prompt-compliance problem

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You add a 'faithfulness' metric that decomposes each RAG answer into atomic claims and checks whether every claim is supported by the retrieved context, the way RAGAS does. One answer scores a perfect 1.0, yet a domain expert marks it factually wrong. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The retrieved context itself contained the wrong information, and the answer faithfully reflected it
A bug in the faithfulness metric, because a fully grounded answer cannot be factually wrong
The model ignored the context and answered from its parametric knowledge
The claim-decomposition step merged distinct claims and hid the error
mcq.rationale: Faithfulness measures whether claims are supported by the provided context, not whether they are true in the world. A perfect score with a wrong answer means the context was wrong and the answer echoed it faithfully -- a retrieval or source-quality problem, not a groundedness failure. Had the model relied on parametric knowledge instead of the context, its claims would not be entailed and faithfulness would drop.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Conflates groundedness (support by context) with real-world factual correctness
Describes the ungrounded case, which would lower faithfulness rather than yield 1.0
Invents a decomposition artifact instead of accepting that the metric measured exactly what it should

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: In a grounded QA system the retriever returns no passage above your relevance threshold for the user's question. To keep the answer grounded, what should the generation step do?
options: Answer from the model's own parametric knowledge so the user still gets a response
Return the top-scoring passage verbatim even though it fell below the threshold
Automatically lower the threshold until at least one passage qualifies
Abstain and tell the user the knowledge base has no supporting evidence
mcq.rationale: Grounding means the answer must rest on retrieved evidence. With nothing above the threshold there is no evidence to ground on, so the faithful behavior is to abstain rather than fall back to parametric memory or force through a passage already judged irrelevant.
misconceptions: Prefers helpfulness over grounding, reintroducing an unverifiable parametric answer
Forces an irrelevant passage in as evidence, fabricating support
Games the threshold to surface passages already judged irrelevant
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You build an LLM-as-judge to score the groundedness of RAG answers. Which judge design measures groundedness specifically, rather than overall answer quality?
options: Give the judge the question and the answer, and ask whether the answer is correct and complete
Give the judge the answer and the retrieved context, and ask whether every claim in the answer is supported by that context
Give the judge the answer and a gold reference answer, and ask how semantically similar they are
Give the judge the question and the retrieved context, and ask whether the context is relevant to the question
mcq.rationale: Groundedness is a property of the answer relative to the context it was generated from: every claim must be supported by that context. Correctness against the question measures accuracy, similarity to a gold answer measures reference overlap, and question-vs-context measures retrieval relevance -- none of them test whether the answer is entailed by the context.
misconceptions: Confuses groundedness with end-to-end answer correctness
CORRECT
Confuses groundedness with reference-based similarity to a gold answer
Confuses groundedness (answer vs context) with retrieval relevance (question vs context)

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: A contract-analysis assistant must display a verbatim supporting quote beneath each answer. With free-form generation the 'quotes' sometimes appear nowhere in the cited document. Which design most reliably guarantees every displayed quote is a real span of the source?
options: Instruct the model to 'copy the quote exactly, do not paraphrase,' with a few-shot example
Increase chunk overlap so the model has more surrounding text to quote from
Diff the generated quote against the document and auto-correct any mismatch
Have the model return a chunk id and character offsets, and let the application slice the quote from the stored source
mcq.rationale: The only way to guarantee a displayed quote exists in the source is to keep the model from authoring the quote text: the model selects a location (chunk id plus character offsets) and the application extracts the actual characters. Copy-exactly prompts still route the text through generation, where it can drift, and overlap or post-hoc diffing never guarantees an exact, real span.
misconceptions: Trusts prompt discipline to stop generative drift when copying text
Mistakes more surrounding context for a guarantee that the emitted text is verbatim
Patches mismatches after the fact instead of removing generation from the quoting path
CORRECT

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your unsupported-claim detector runs an NLI model over `(retrieved_context, claim)` pairs and flags a claim as a hallucination only when the model predicts `contradiction`. Hallucinated claims keep slipping through. What is the flaw?
options: Fabricated claims are usually `neutral` w.r.t. the context, not `contradiction`, so flagging only `contradiction` misses them; treat anything that is not `entailment` as unsupported
NLI models truncate long retrieved contexts, so the entailment labels are unreliable
The premise and hypothesis are reversed; NLI should be run as `(claim, retrieved_context)`
Each claim should be verified against the gold reference answer rather than the retrieved context
mcq.rationale: For a claim to be grounded the context must entail it. Hallucinations usually add information the context never mentions, so the NLI label is `neutral`, not `contradiction`; flagging only contradictions misses them entirely. The correct rule is unsupported = anything that is not `entailment`, covering both `neutral` and `contradiction`.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Blames context-length truncation for what is a labeling-logic error
Misreads the NLI direction; the context is correctly the premise and the claim the hypothesis
Confuses grounding against the retrieved context with correctness against a gold answer, which is unavailable at inference

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: You raise your RAG retriever's `top_k` from 5 to 20 and re-run the same labeled evaluation set, changing nothing else about the index or ranking. Which statement about the retrieval metrics is guaranteed by construction?
options: `Precision@20` is greater than or equal to `Precision@5` for every query
`F1@20` is greater than or equal to `F1@5`, since recall can only rise
`Recall@20` is greater than or equal to `Recall@5` for every query
`MRR@20` is strictly greater than `MRR@5`
mcq.rationale: Raising `top_k` only lengthens the ranked list, so the top-20 set is a superset of the top-5 set and every relevant document found at k=5 is still counted at k=20 -- `Recall@k` is monotonically non-decreasing in `k`. `Precision@k` has a growing denominator, `F1` blends precision with recall, and `MRR` reflects only the first hit's position, so each can stay flat or fall; none is guaranteed to improve.
misconceptions: Assumes precision inherits recall's monotonicity in `k`; adding lower-ranked hits usually dilutes it
Expects `F1` to track recall alone, ignoring that a falling precision term can pull the harmonic mean down
CORRECT
Believes a larger cutoff must improve the first-hit rank, but it is unchanged when a relevant document already lies within the smaller cutoff

items.competency: LLM, Prompt, RAG and Knowledge Engineering

mcq.stem: Your team built the retrieval golden set by having annotators label only the passages the current production retriever returned in its top 10. You now evaluate a new embedding model against that set with `Recall@10`, and it scores lower than the incumbent. What is the most likely methodological flaw in this comparison?
options: `Recall@10` is the wrong metric here; `Precision@10` would compare the two retrievers fairly
The new model is overfitting the evaluation queries, which is why its recall dropped
The two retrievers cannot share one `qrels` file unless their embeddings are L2-normalized to the same scale
The judgments are incomplete: passages that only the new model surfaces were never labeled, so they count as non-relevant and unfairly penalize it
mcq.rationale: Because annotators judged only what the incumbent surfaced, the `qrels` are incomplete. When the new model retrieves a genuinely relevant passage that was never labeled, it is scored as non-relevant, so `Recall@10` understates the new model and flatters the incumbent -- a classic pooling bias. Switching to `Precision@10` reads the same faulty labels, and the effect has nothing to do with overfitting or vector normalization. The fix is to pool and judge the union of both systems' top results before comparing.
misconceptions: Thinks changing the metric removes the bias, but the missing relevant judgments are absent from the `qrels` whichever metric reads them
Mistakes a labeling artifact for a training problem and reverses overfitting's direction, which would inflate eval-query scores rather than depress them
Invents an embedding-normalization prerequisite; `qrels` validity depends on judgment coverage, not vector scaling
CORRECT

code.title: Constraint-based model selection
code.prompt:
Implement `choose_model_c2_5(candidates, max_latency_ms, min_quality)` for Data validation, quality & leakage checks. Candidates: `{name,latency_ms,quality,cost}`. Keep candidates meeting thresholds, pick min cost; tie by higher quality, then lower latency, then name. Return name or None.

Signature: def choose_model_c2_5(candidates: list[dict], max_latency_ms: int, min_quality: float) -> str | None
code.reference_solution:
def choose_model_c2_5(candidates,max_latency_ms,min_quality):
    v=[c for c in candidates if c['latency_ms']<=max_latency_ms and c['quality']>=min_quality]
    if not v: return None
    v.sort(key=lambda c:(c['cost'],-c['quality'],c['latency_ms'],c['name']))
    return v[0]['name']

code.title: Constraint-based model selection
code.prompt:
Implement `choose_model_c8_2(candidates, max_latency_ms, min_quality)` for Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA). Candidates: `{name,latency_ms,quality,cost}`. Keep candidates meeting thresholds, pick min cost; tie by higher quality, then lower latency, then name. Return name or None.

Signature: def choose_model_c8_2(candidates: list[dict], max_latency_ms: int, min_quality: float) -> str | None
code.reference_solution:
def choose_model_c8_2(candidates,max_latency_ms,min_quality):
    v=[c for c in candidates if c['latency_ms']<=max_latency_ms and c['quality']>=min_quality]
    if not v: return None
    v.sort(key=lambda c:(c['cost'],-c['quality'],c['latency_ms'],c['name']))
    return v[0]['name']

code.title: Constraint-based model selection
code.prompt:
Implement `choose_model_c9_1(candidates, max_latency_ms, min_quality)` for Cloud architecture & compute selection. Candidates: `{name,latency_ms,quality,cost}`. Keep candidates meeting thresholds, pick min cost; tie by higher quality, then lower latency, then name. Return name or None.

Signature: def choose_model_c9_1(candidates: list[dict], max_latency_ms: int, min_quality: float) -> str | None
code.reference_solution:
def choose_model_c9_1(candidates,max_latency_ms,min_quality):
    v=[c for c in candidates if c['latency_ms']<=max_latency_ms and c['quality']>=min_quality]
    if not v: return None
    v.sort(key=lambda c:(c['cost'],-c['quality'],c['latency_ms'],c['name']))
    return v[0]['name']

code.title: Canary rollout decision
code.prompt:
Implement `canary_decision_c9_11(baseline_error, canary_error, canary_requests, min_requests, max_delta)` for Resilience & failure handling. Return `hold` if insufficient traffic, `rollback` if error delta exceeds max_delta, else `promote`.

code.reference_solution:
def canary_decision_c9_11(baseline_error,canary_error,canary_requests,min_requests,max_delta):
    if canary_requests<min_requests: return 'hold'
    if (canary_error-baseline_error)>max_delta: return 'rollback'
    return 'promote'

code.title: Constraint-based model selection
code.prompt:
Implement `choose_model_c10_2(candidates, max_latency_ms, min_quality)` for Execution & state architecture. Candidates: `{name,latency_ms,quality,cost}`. Keep candidates meeting thresholds, pick min cost; tie by higher quality, then lower latency, then name. Return name or None.

Signature: def choose_model_c10_2(candidates: list[dict], max_latency_ms: int, min_quality: float) -> str | None
code.reference_solution:
def choose_model_c10_2(candidates,max_latency_ms,min_quality):
    v=[c for c in candidates if c['latency_ms']<=max_latency_ms and c['quality']>=min_quality]
    if not v: return None
    v.sort(key=lambda c:(c['cost'],-c['quality'],c['latency_ms'],c['name']))
    return v[0]['name']
